The 14 Psalm. To the end. A psalm of David, which teaches the punishment of the wicked and the return of the nations to God from the captivity of the devil. The wicked says in his heart, (v.1) i.e. because he denies God, he is corrupt in his ways. Again, the wicked is the devil who sows polytheism in the human heart in order that he might defile it with iniquity. The Lord looketh from heaven, (v.2) i.e. although he thus sees and fills everything, it is said of him that he looked as one being about to become man, and therefore he looked by the prophets as by windows and taught and commanded, and when this availed nothing, he descended and became man. Those that eat my people (with) the eating of bread, (v.4) i.e. they were eating his people, who were persuading them to worship the creature instead of the creator. Again the scribes and Pharisees were eating the people of the Lord and were taking the wages of teaching unlawfully, because they were not fearing the Lord. There they were in fear where there was no fear, (v.5) i.e. because the nations were afraid of demons and idol-priests, and were sacrificing their children. Again, the people of the Lord were afraid because of the threat of the scribes and Pharisees and were bringing offerings. Again, at the time of the appearance of our Savior men were fearing God, not the fear of the threat of the law of Moses, but fear
that is becoming free-born men. Because God is in the generation of the righteous, (v.5) i.e. of those who were made righteous through his appearance. They have put to shame the counsel of the needy, (v.6) i.e. the heathen who continued in unbelief, persecuted the needy in spirit and those who believe in the Messiah. The captivity of Zion, (v.7) i.e. of the nations and the whole world by the devil and sheol. Jacob will exult, (v.7) i.e. the just and the righteous and the saints. And Israel will rejoice, (v.7) i.e. the prophets of Israel. Concerning the same psalm according to the LXX. This psalm alludes to the coming of our Lord in the flesh. The fool says in his heart, (v.1) i.e. he denounces the heathen who worship idols. The Lord looketh, (v.2) i.e. as he that looks from above, whence he looks, is below by the power of sight, so also the Messiah, remaining in heaven in the divine state, was by the power of the dispensation upon the earth. To see whether there be any who is intelligent, (v.2) i.e. if there is an intelligent one, he will see that in the beauty of the creatures he may know their creator. All of them have gone astray, (v.3) i.e. all of the earth has wandered away to impurity and from the side of virtue. And have been rejected, (v.3) i.e. they were corrupted; because they led astray, they were corrupted and there was not a remnant of goodness left in them. So the priests of the Jews went astray in the evil against the Messiah. Open sepulchres are their throats, i.e.
because they are perverting the truth of the words to blasphemy. With their tongues they deceive, i.e. lying he calls deceit. The mouth is full of curses and bitterness, i.e. a tongue ready for curses, that is, slanders they have. Those that eat my people (with) the eating of bread, (v.4) i.e. a man eats his neighbor when he harms him, as (we read): if ye bite and eat one another, see that ye be not devoured one of another. They give thought to the oppression of the needy as to eating of bread. Hence and they do not cry to the Lord, (v.4) and although they should cry, God does not hear them, because they continue in oppression. There they are in fear where there is no fear, (v.5) i.e. fearing lest the Messiah be stolen from the grave, they guarded the dead the one. For who feels fear of theft and flight of a dead one, such as they felt? In the generation of the righteous, (v.5) i.e. he calls the perfection in deed of the just or the perfection of will of holy men. The counsel of the poor ye have put to shame, (v.5) i.e. the poor he calls the prophets and apostles for they were needy of spirit and strangers to pride and mingled with the needy. Again, the poor he calls the Messiah who was poor for our sakes, tasting death in the flesh. The Jews sought to put him to shame, thinking
concerning him that he was a contemptible dead man. Who will give salvation out of Zion? (v.7) i.e. he desires that the Messiah appear, the forgiver of sins, and offers the prayer that from the seed of David and from Zion the Messiah appear who is salvation. When the Lord will turn the captivity, (v.7) i.e. those people who were taken captive by the devil the Lord calls by means of the hymn.

The 15 Psalm. This psalm teaches man to prepare for a blessed end and for the tabernacle of God and for the mansions above. The tabernacle and the mountain he calls heaven and the Jerusalem above. Worthy of these is he that does the things that are written in the psalm. Concerning it according to the LXX: O Lord, who will sojourn in thy tabernacle? (v.1) i.e. a sojourning is a temporary dwelling; the word shows that while man is living in the flesh, it is meet that he be a sojourner until he dwell in the places of that world. And who will lodge on thy (holy) mountain?,(v.1) i.e. the lodging-place and tabernacle he calls the body. Who therefore will look upon the flesh as a strange (land)? For if we bring the fruits of repentance, the body will truly be a lodging-place for God. At first God will sojourn in us and after that we will be a lodging-place to him through the perfection of excellence. Again he calls the lodging-place and the mountain of God the city of heaven and those who are sojourners in the tabernacle by a moral life, i.e. in the church, will enter the Jerusalem above. Again who he places because of the multitude of those that are to be corrected. The tabernacle he calls the body and human life; the mountain he calls the kingdom of heaven; a mountain- because of its height and
because it is situated above; holy- because no unclean one dwells there. When a man overcomes this flesh without passion, having sojourned in it as if in a strange (land) and mortified its members, he will be considered worthy of the shining mountain concerning which the apostle says: you are brought to the mountain of the living God. Who will dwell in thy tabernacle? and the rest, and the Lord answers him: he who walketh blamelessly and worketh righteousness (v.2). In this psalm he teaches those things by, which we may become worthy of a blessed end: first, if we walk the blameless way which is the Messiah; second, if we do righteousness; third, if we make our hearts a house of truth; fourth, if we do not possess a deceitful tongue; fifth, that we do not do evil to our neighbor; sixth, that we do not boastfully harm our neighbor; seventh, that we do not admire external appearance, but even if an evil one be rich, that we despise him, and if a poor one be good, that we praise him; eighth, that we do not break the faith of oaths; ninth, that we do not take increase; tenth, that we do not accept a bribe. He that directs his life according to these without wavering, will be blessed. Who walks blamelessly, (v.2) i.e. he who is perfect in virtues. And who worketh righteousness, (v.2) i.e. he who in his bodily deeds conforms to holiness. And he does not say: who walked, but who is walking, and not who worked, but who is working because one act does not make holiness complete, but is meet that during the whole lifetime we strive for excellence. And he who speaks the truth in his heart, (v.3) i.e. it is meet that not only with the truth but that, as it were, of the fountain of the action we
make the heart; it is incumbent first that we be truthful in the heart and then with the tongue: from the fullness of the heart the mouth speaketh. (Who is) not deceitful with his tongue and does not do (evil) to his neighbor, (v.2,3) i.e. it is meet for man to be of good repute before God and men in word and deeds. Bribe against his neighbor, (v.3) i.e. neighbor he calls everyone because by nature we are all alike. For it is not becoming that with anything, great or small, we harm someone, and that we do not take anything from him wrongfully. That swears to his neighbor and does not deceive, (v.4) i.e. in the beginning he permitted oaths and in the end he abolished them, as the law said: Thou shalt not commit adultery, but the Lord commanded that we do not lust. There are words that have the form of oaths but are not, as when Joseph spoke the dream of Paraoh and Paul: Verily your glory which I have in the Messiah, and God is a witness to me whom I serve, and I call upon God as a witness against my soul, again there knows God who is above everything that I do not lie; this however is faith unblameable. For an oath is a word with the witness of God. His silver does he not give upon usury, (v.5) i.e. silver he calls the word of
teaching. For if they sowed spiritual things thereby that they teach, they obtain bodily things thereby that they will be fed; for the laborer is worthy of his food; however they are not to increase. For they are not to take money which is equal to the mental gifts that were given but only food. Paul did not give for usury, but without wage he preached the gospel. He does not take a bribe against the innocent, (v.5) i.e. every taking of bribe is evil indeed. For fire, he says, will burn the houses of those who receive a bribe, especially (if they take a bribe) against the innocent i.e. against the righteous. For the taking of a bribe eventuates evil.

The 16 Psalm. There is in this a prophecy concerning the resurrection of the Messiah and the calling of the heathen and an accusation concerning the disobedience of Israel. Keep me, O Lord, because in thee have I put my trust, (v.1) i.e. these (words) spoke the Messiah, having assumed the appearance of mankind; he asks that the church might be kept which is his flesh. I said to the Lord: my Lord art thou, (v.1) i.e. because the son took upon himself the likeness of a servant, he says the word for us. Again I said, i.e. the nations speak thus, having become members of the household of faith by confession, to him who is Lord by nature. My good is from thee.... to the saints, (v.3) i.e. to the apostles. Who are on the earth, (v.3) i.e. in the church. And the illustrious, (v.3) i.e. through the miracles which they did. In whom is all of my desire, (v.3) i.e. because they fulfill his desire, he desires them. Their sufferings shall be multiplied, (v.4) i.e.
oppressions and persecutions and slayings because of the gospel message. And not will I offer their drink-offerings, (v.4) i.e. of the people of the Jews; because they oppressed the apostles, they will not be worthy of the drink-offering of the blood of God which drops a blessing upon the bruises of the world. And I will not remember their names, (v.4) i.e. the names of the crucifiers because he said: I know you not, and he has not written their names in the book of life. The Lord is the portion of my inheritance, (v.5) i.e. my father has given me the nations as an inheritance, as (we read): Ask of me and I will give, and this (happened) because I was obedient unto death. For cup he names death, as (we read): My father, if it be possible, let this cup pass by me. Thou hast returned unto me..., (v.5) i.e. paradise from which this nature was expelled for whom I am bringing in a petition, in order that I might return to paradise. The lines are fallen to me in excellent ones, (v.6) i.e. the lines he calls the bonds of love which he had with the church; even those are the excellent ones who in love serve him and please him. I will bless the Lord who has made me king, (v.7) i.e. who will make me king over his church. In the nights my reins instruct me, (v.7) i.e. reins he calls the thoughts; the night (he calls) ignorance, i.e. in the ignorance and darkness of this world I am moving about because I shall enlighten it, as (we read):light shineth into darkness. I will place the Lord before me, (v.8)
i.e. providentially he says these (words) because he became man. Lord he calls the father. Because of this my heart rejoices, (v.9) i.e. because of the deliverance of the lost sheep. And also my flesh shall dwell....., (v.9) i.e. because when I am buried my body shall not be puffed up and corrupted and give forth putrid odor and worms swarm from it. The body that suffers these is not at rest, for mine, because it shall not be corrupted, is at rest. In the Greek: incorruptibility (was) in the grave until the soul returned to him and he arose on the third day. Because thou hast not left my soul, (v.10) i.e. these refer to the son as Peter expounded. Thou wilt show me thy ways of life, (v.11) i.e. because I will show to the world the way of immortality when in me as in the beginning they see the resurrection and incorruptibility. And I shall be satisfied by the joy of..., (v.11) i.e. and this he says because he became man, because he assumed the appearance of mankind in order that we through his poverty might become rich. For we are those who are about to be counted worthy of delight, such as this, and of joy unceasing, and not he who is God by nature and is inseparable from the father. According to the LXX: upon it the inscription concerning the resurrection, is written because in it he speaks the mystery of the resurrection of our Lord. Again the inscription concerning the column, i.e. as the signs which are in wars against enemies are on a column for an extended memorial,
so also a great sign of the victory of our Lord which he accomplished over death, is inscribed in the prophetical writings as if on a column. Of my good thou hast no need, (v.2) i.e. for he is not in need of legal service and earthly goods, but he desires faith from us and knowledge of the truth. To these saints that are on his earth, (v.3) i.e. the saints of God dwell in his land which is the Jerusalem above and in heaven is their life although they are still dwelling on the earth. The apostles and the saints he made marvelous, (v.3) i.e. he showed his graces which are the miracles, that is, by sacraments and not through miracles and signs with which he confirmed his disciples. Their weaknesses are multiplied, (v.4) i.e. of the nations in error. And when they were called to the truth, he says: They hastened, (v.4) i.e. readily they accepted the faith. In a different way: for when they often sought to deceive the Messiah, they became sick; finally when he had left, they hastened to the cross and the passion. I will (not) gather their assemblies, (v.4) i.e. of the Jews. Neither will I remember their names, (v.4) i.e. for any reason whatever. Of blood, (v.4) i.e. because in much blood and slaying of prophets, and in the end of the heir, they were taken. Again: I will not gather, i.e. although the prophets and apostles were killed and their blood was
shed, I will not gather their assemblies with the blood of these, but with the blood of the Messiah by which they were saved from the conversation of their fathers. I will not gather their assemblies, i.e. because of the blood which was shed wickedly. Stephen they stoned and also James they killed and many others. I will not remember their names, (v.4) i.e. at first they were called unclean nations and heathen, now I will not remember these names, but instead of them they will be called the called and saints. Thou art he who is restoring to me my inheritance, (v.5) i.e. thou art he who will restore those nations who were taken as a spoil by the devil; when he will go forth from the grave as a bridegroom from the bridal-chamber, he will espouse the church saying to the apostles: go and teach all nations. The lines are fallen to me in excellent ones, (v.6) i.e. formerly the lot and inheritance was Israel, when it had fallen because of its iniquity, another portion and other lots and shares were given to thee in place of these in excellent ones. And also my inheritance is excellent, (v.6) i.e. the church of the gentiles is excellent and with the cords of love it is strongly bound fast and joined to the Messiah, and it is called excellent because of its virtuous manner of life. And also during the nights my reins instruct me, (v.7) i.e. from the reins proceed the seed by which a child is brought into existence; so also from the powers of the soul thoughts go out from which the fruits of virtue are born, and he says of him who has pure modesty, that he
even continues until the night, and from his reins, contained in pure thought, to let flow forth spiritual and bodily seeds. And he is at my right hand that I may not be moved, (v.8) i.e. in as much as he is God, he sustains and holds everything; in as much as he is man, it is proper for him that he should be at the right hand of the Lord that he may not be moved; from voluntary poverty he will not shrink because of providence. As he died in the flesh and prepared a resurrection for us through his death, so also at the right hand he receives the Lord in order that he might prepare this for us. My flesh shall dwell in hope, (v.9) i.e. the flesh rested in hope, pointing to the resurrection that was about to take place. And again where shall he dwell? -upon the cross and in the grave; and in what hope? i.e. of the resurrection. I shall be satisfied in the joy of thy countenance, (v.11) i.e. the countenance and the image of the father is the son.

The 17 Psalm. Hear, O Lord, O Holy One, and consider my petition, (v.1) i.e. this psalm was sung by him impersonating him who is made perfect in God. Thou hast tried me and hast not found wickedness in me, (v.3) i.e. blasphemy against God. Thou hast upheld my steps in thy paths, (v.5) i.e. in thy commands. Do a miracle, (v.7) i.e. in that thou savest. In another way: all of the things in this psalm are understood concerning the Messiah who for our sakes became needy and was obedient unto death, who committed no sin and neither was guile found in his mouth, who was reviled, but did not revile, for he is the holy one of
the father, who was the miracle in the world because he was incarnated and was born without seed of a virgin, her chastity being preserved, who fled to Egypt, who was glorified by the angels, who suffered, who died, who arose, who wrought the miracle that he save the world. From these sinners who despoil me, (v.9) i.e. the devil and the Jews who hoped that, having laid him low in death, he would remain dead and would not rise. From the dead who die, (v.14) i.e. in sin. By the hand of the Lord, (v.14) i.e. because they killed themselves by sin, he excludes them from the life that is in him. The dead of the pit, (v.14) i.e. those who die by judgment and are imprisoned in a dark place of torture. Pit he calls the dread and gloomy depth. Others: (the word) is disgrace. Thou wilt divide them in life, (v.14) i.e. and these (things happen) when they divided against the Lord in life, i.e. when he comes and makes division among them. Again when they are alive in the resurrection, he will elevate the righteous to heaven, the wicked, however, he will cast out into sheol. Their belly is full of thy treasures, (v.14) i.e. when thou shalt gladden them in the mansions of the kingdom. The children shall be satisfied, (v.14) i.e. the disciples shall be gladdened with blessings. And they will leave the rest to their children, (v.14) i.e. to those who through them believe and are servants and hirelings, and therefore the remnant will come to them, but not everything as the perfect ones, the joy of the children and the hirelings and
the servants being not the same. I.....in righteousness, (v.15) i.e. the prophet prays that they may have a portion with them. And I will be satisfied when I am awakened, (v.15) i.e. when I shall be awakened from the grave, I shall be satisfied with blessings like them. Concerning the psalm according the LXX: Hear, O Lord, my righteousness, (v.1) righteousness he calls the gospel dispensation which he loved and for which he longed. Again he petitions God that not of words but by deeds may be his excellence which he calls righteousness. Hear my prayer, (v.1) i.e. not with deceitful lips, i.e. with pure lips I offer my request, not thinking of other things. I speak other things, to be sure, but with pleasure I have a tongue that praises. For God hears that prayer which is free of deceptive lips; the word that goes forth through the lips, thou wilt hear. Three (things) he asks by these (words), which are placed first, having previously placed before these two (this) that he is virtuous. From thy presence may my sentence proceed, (v.2) i.e. he does not want to be judged by men but by God, because God does not judge (moved) by a bribe or by adulation nor by enmity, but even while judging, he is moved by compassion. May thine eyes see righteousness, (v.2) because with you there is no crookedness but straightness of judgment. Again his eyes he calls the disciples. For we are members of his body. He prays therefore that they may see uprightness. Thou hast tried me and visited me at night, (v.3) i.e. he visits at night in order to dispel the darkness of sin, bringing in the light as the spiritual sun. And thou hast tried me and hast not
found in me......, (v.3) i.e. the proving he calls the trials by which the souls of the righteous are tested. Not have passed over my mouth....., (v.3) i.e. thou wilt understand these (things) also as if impersonated by our Savior. For his mouth did not speak the work of men; I have not come to judge the world but to save the world. Because of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard paths, (v.4) i.e. because of thy commandments I have entered the straight and narrow gate. The paths that lead to excellence appear hard, such as this: he that strikes thee upon thy cheek, turn to him the other. Perfect my steps in thy paths that they may not waver, (v.5) i.e. as a man cannot see without light, so also (he can not) walk uprightly unless he receives power from God. The paths are the good deeds, that is to say, the excellent ones through which a man is brought to me. From those who rise up against thy right hand, (v.7) i.e. the right hand of the father is the son. There arose against him the heathen, worshipping idols and forsaking the creator, and there arose against him the Jews in as much as they would not acknowledge that they knew the mystery of the prophets that they prophesied of him, but they pursued him; there arose against him, furthermore, the heretics, thereby that they regarded him who was equal to the father by nature, as a creature. Keep me as the apple of the eye, (v.8) i.e. the righteous, the eyes of whose soul are enlightened, seek this and they petition that they may be protected
from those demons who endeavor to blind the eyes of the soul. And hide me in the shadow of thy wings, (v.9) i.e. the powers of his providence he calls wings. Sinners who despoil......, (v.9) i.e. the demons he calls sinners who despoil and make miserable those who are caught by them. My enemies hold against me, (v.9) i.e. he refers to the demons. They hold back their fat, (v.9) i.e. he refers to the carnal-minded and those who are filled with much pleasure and joy as if with fat and fatness. Some name fatness an abundance of days and beautiful possessions; it appears to me that he calls it bread thus, when they hold back natural charity and do not show philanthropy. They speak arrogant things, They speak a boast, (v.10) i.e. boast he calls the falling away from God to injustice of judgment; having obtained these, they are eager to lead them into sin who err. Having cast me out, now they surround me, (v.11) in the Peshitta: they praised me and now they surrounded me, i.e. they cast me out; they judged me and surrounded me diligently. In order that they might cast me into the earth, (v.11) i.e. while I was still living. They set their eyes, (v.11) i.e. rather than the blessedness that is in heaven the demons desired carnal things; they turned aside to the earth; from here they incite even us to turn aside. They are like lions, (v.12) i.e. the demons run after the manner of lions to capture the saints. And as a young
lion, (v.12) i.e. Satan hides himself and deceptively lays ruses; they do not wage war with us openly but secretly. Arise, O Lord, (v.13) i.e. he prays to God that he may trip up the enemies in order that they may fall from their intentions; for when we hearken to God after the manner of sheep, then he also will arise as a shepherd, and the beasts shall be caught. Save my soul from the wicked, (v.13) i.e. from the devil; from evil men. From the sword, (v.13) i.e. the Greek is and from the spear, The word of God is sharper than a two-edged sword, lest the enemies take it and smite us with it. He teaches further that sometimes enemies take the words of God which are from Scripture and by them they in turn overcome the simple. Because of this he prays that his spear may be saved from the enemies of God and therefore the Greek says: thy spear from the enemies of thy hand. O Lord, from the few of the earth, (v.14) i.e. few he calls the holy, as (we read): many are called, but few are chosen. Divide them therefore in their life, (v.14) i.e. separate the evil from the saints, and this is the same as: thou wilt divine them in life, (v.14) i.e. he will remove the few, i.e. the holy, from them and exalt them. Their belly is filled with thy hidden things, (v.14) i.e. with all the precious things they were pleased and afterwards they kicked up their heels, in order that
they might also transgress the law. In the Syriac: from the dead that die by thy hands, O Lord, etc; in the LXX: Lord, from the few; he prays also in this manner that they may be divided. Of thy secret things there is filled their belly, the satiety of swine. The children shall be filled and leave, etc. (v.14) i.e. he reproves them as rejecters of goodness because when the children had received blessings from God, they did not transmit the excellence to their families, but the remnant of evil in the place of portions they transmitted. I therefore shall appear before thee in righteousness, (v.15) i.e. through excellence, that is righteousness, we shall be worthy to appear in the presence of the father which is the son. I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear to me, (v.15) i.e. for when thy name is spread widely, i.e. thy glory, under the heaven, then there will appear to me thy son, i.e. thy face.

The 18 Psalm. The title: by the youth David, i.e. he did not call him king or prophet, but a youth, because there is a boast for him in this, not being called a youth from stature, but from excellence and heroism, and as a youth, i.e. a son, speaks with confidently with his father, so David (speaks) to his Lord as with a friend and father. According to the translation of the LXX youth was of the text. He speaks the words of this song, i.e. he did not speak a song of praise because, being old, he spoke it, not playing on the harp or on the
tambourine, but (as) conversing with God, for to an old man a musical instrument is an annoyance of his soul, and it is not pleasant. On the day on which he saved him from his enemies, i.e. from foreign enemies and from Saul he saved him, i.e. from his visitations that he would not suffer those (things) that were like those of that one. Again from the hand of Saul, i.e. from his power and his sons and his sons of sons and his family. I will love thee, O Lord, my strength, (v.1) i.e. strength he calls the Lord, holding up to shame the weak strength of creatures. My refuge, (v.2) i.e. in as much as God had been to him a defence and a strong hedge. My savior, (v.2) i.e. in as much as through God I shall escape from the enemies. God is my helper, (v.2) i.e. who was to help me. My succourer, (v.2) i.e. in as much as in the time of war he succoured me. Horn of (my) salvation, (v.2) i.e. by derivation from those beasts that with horns take revenge on enemies. A horn, furthermore, is called the Messiah, as Zachariah says: He hath raised up for us a horn, etc. He is called a horn because that Messiah, of whom were the patriarchs, was of patriarchs and kings whose genealogy was linked with him. A horn he is called and a kingdom as (we read): he will give strength among our kings and raise the horn of his anointed one. Again there was a horn of salvation by means of the cross, for there is nothing that is more dreadful for the demons than the cross. I will call unto the Lord, and
from (my enemies) (v.3) i.e. not: I am crying, but I will cry, for he does not yet know the manner of true calling; we learn (it) when the Only One appointed apostles, saying: whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, ye shall receive. Enemies he here calls the demons who inwardly surround the soul. The pangs of death, (v.4) and of sheol, (v.5) he calls the many kinds of trials; dangers (he calls) the bringing about of death. For as there are pangs at birth, so many dangers lead to death. The torrents of ungodliness, (v.4) i.e. the streams of evil he calls torrents. Again the sudden accidents (he calls the evil deeds of the enemies. The snares (of death) prevented me, (v.5) i.e. snares he names those temptations that are hidden and not manifest to everyone. And to God I cried, (v.6) i.e. man cannot be freed from evil unless he cry to God. And he heard from his temple, (v.6) i.e. not the one in Jerusalem does he mean; it had not yet been built, but the one in heaven he calls temple. And my clamor is before him, (v.6) i.e. clamor is either before the eyes or (it comes) in the ears; that before the eyes, on the one hand, that he will have pity; in the ears, on the other hand, that he will hear and accept. The earth was moved and was in a tremor, (v.7) i.e. all those who dwell on the elements of the earth were shaken and moved and every Hellenic and barbarian hearing was filled with the rumor of the coming into the flesh of our Lord. For if God, looking upon it from above, made it to tremble how would it not tremble when he comes
down upon it in the flesh. The foundations of the mountains were rent, (v.7) i.e. the mountains are the evil powers that grow alarmed at the praise of God. Their foundations he calls the thoughts which are in the depth. They quaked because his anger was provoked against them, (v.7) i.e. he was angry and extinguished their fire with which formerly they had set men aflame, and (as) a sign of this he puts down smoke (v.8). There went up smoke in his anger, (v.8) i.e. he directs his anger at first against the heinous like smoke; when fire is about to be kindled, smoke goes up; when fire is kindled and consumes pieces of wood, coals should be blazing; when he was about to go up like smoke against the mountains, i.e. the demons who are the foundations and the powers, there was kindled the fire of that word that was made flesh, and it consumed them like matter that is of no use and made them full of coals, i.e. anger and punishment, and their fire will not be quenched. Again fire from his countenance, (v.8) i.e. fire he calls the glow of the holy spirit by which men that are in the spirit appear to glow. Again to fire he compares the holy apostles. Again as smoke goes up from a lamp which burns, after it is extinguished, in the same way the demons at first are compared to fire and they set aflame the souls of men and cause them to burn, and because their light was extinguished, they show the smoke that goes up from it. The light from his countenance, (v.8) i.e. for these (things) the son of God puts into effect visibly against the invisible and hostile powers, (and) extinguishing their fire with a fire that is more excellent and
powerful. And coals were kindled by him, (v.8) i.e. coals sometimes signify the torment, sometimes the fiery and glowing words that purify the thoughts of the soul. He bent down the heavens and came down, (v.9) i.e. he bent the heavens down in order to join the earth to the heavens and give to those (who are) below fellowship with those above. This would not have been so, except he had come down and been incarnated. A dark cloud was under (his feet), (v.9) i.e. the flesh he calls thick darkness, this conceals the coming of God which in the end took place among us. He rides upon cherubim, (v.10) i.e. cherubim and wings he calls that cloud that received him and concealed him from their eyes. He flew upon the wings of the wind, (v.10) i.e. he likens the cherubim to the wind because of the velocity of flight. Again, he rides upon the cherubim, i.e. the word cherubim is understood regarding the great amount of learning, for where there is much and pure knowledge, from there, riding by means of lofty intelligence, he flies. He flies upon the wings of the wind, (v.10) i.e. by reason of his providence he rides upon the tumultuous winds, i.e. upon his majesty, and governs them according to his will. Again he calls wind the wise men who through the spirit are exalted and in a spiritual way are called knowledge(s); upon the wings of these, God, having taken his seat, flies. Their wings are exalted and loftily soar-
ing intelligences. He made darkness his secret place, (v.11) i.e. the concealing of the mystery of his mode of life with the flesh he calls darkness, for they know not his power, not even the demons (do). Around him is his tabernacle, (v.11) the church or heaven or the temple on earth or the light about him, just as him who is enclosed by a tabernacle, no one can see, if he enters in by the curtain of difficulty of comprehension. Dark waters in the clouds of the air, (v.11) i.e. the clouds are the prophets to whom air was the operations of the spirits, whose waters had been dark, i.e. they were not manifest before the coming of our Savior, for the Jews did not believe that a virgin would conceive and give birth. From the brightness, clouds went before him, (v.12) i.e. the light of his manifestation made manifest the prophecy regarding him. Hail and coals of fire, (v.12) i.e. torturing powers were brought against the enemies of the new preaching, the devil and demons and evil men; divine wrath therefore, in the likeness of hail and fire, shatters and sets on fire their power. And the Lord thundered out of the heavens, (v.13) i.e. because he named the clouds the saints, he compared the thunder to the preaching by them; for not in Judea was it preached, but in all the earth. He sent his arrows and scattered them, (v.14) i.e. arrows and lightnings (v.14) he calls the speed of the anger that he brings against the
enemies. Again he calls the apostles and evangelists, arrows and lightnings: arrows, on the one hand, in as much as they wound the heart of the devil; lightnings, on the other hand, in as much as they enlighten those that are dark in sin, and teach them the true faith. The springs of water appeared, (v.15) i.e. the springs he calls the prophets in as much as they pour forth the saving word. And the foundations of the world were uncovered, (v.15) i.e. the Book of Moses he calls the foundation and the lintel by which God is known to be one and the creator. Again the apostles are the springs and the same are the foundations of the world, not of the land of Juda, but of all the world, for they appeared in all the earth. Again the springs are the precepts of the gospel from which flow divine teachings. By thy rebuke, O Lord, and the blast (of the breath of thy anger), (v.15) i.e. creation was not freed of idolatry by the power of the apostles but by the power of God, for God does no more bring torment with sin, otherwise everything would perish, and this happens when he breathes the breath of his anger. He sent from above and drew me out, (v.16) i.e. for in truth he saved the human race when he sent the gift of the spirit to us from heaven. He took me out of many waters, (v.16) i.e. by means of the many waters of baptism; they are not many in quantity but by (their) efficacy; rather, however, also by its magnitude the sacrament of ablution fills all the earth. Others: he calls the waters the trials, and those trials are (my) mighty enemies, (v.17) i.e. the heretics who with cunning wisdom overcome the simple and turn them to their
perverted teaching. Others: the calls the mighty enemies the demons, for because we subject ourselves to them, we give them power over us, and they also grow strong, for they had been weaker than we through the royal image in us. They came upon me at the time of my ill-treatment, (v.18) i.e. Peshitta: my debility, i.e. it refers to the insurrection of Absalom against him after (his) sin. Symmachus interprets the ill-treatment(s) as debility, which is infirmity of the soul, which was by reason of sin. And the Lord was my stay, (v.18) i.e. when I would have fallen after the sin, the Lord stood by me and supported me when he sent me Nathan, the prophet, and when I was called again from ruin by him, he raised me up and guided me aright. Furthermore, when the first Adam had fallen and the race had been corrupted, he made himself for an example when he became the new Adam. He brought me forth to a wide place, (v.19) i.e. from the straits of the law and the scripture he brought us forth to the wideness of the gospel. Again when the Lord is a man's sustainer, he brings him out of the straits of affliction, giving him a wide place; in distress a man given a wide place, standing heroically and humbly at his side. The Lord will reward me according to my righteousness, (v.20) i.e. weighing my action in righteousness, as it were in a scale, against my sins, he finds that my righteousnesses are in greater number than my sins, and because of it he rewards me not according to as I sin. And according to the cleanness of my hands (he will reward me), (v.20) i.e. the actual deeds
achieved by an excellent habit, he calls pureness of hands; pure are the hands of those that do not despoil; purer those that give alms. Because I have kept his way, (v.22) i.e. ways he calls the commands in which we have our course with God. All his judgments are before me, (v.22) i.e. although his judgments are not comprehended, yet when they are decreed before us and the matters of his providence are accomplished by the judgment of God, we are pleasing to him. His righteousnesses will not be removed from me, (v.22) i.e. these are the enactment of laws in equity and justice, as (we read): if thou possess a Jewish servant. I will be blameless with him and I will guard myself against (my sins), (v.23) i.e. those that (do not act) from (love to) God but because of praise or any other thing, can be blameless, to be sure, in that which is blameless and without sin to them, but not with God; these, on the other hand, that, because of God, love goodness and not because of anything else, are blameless with God. With the holy thou shalt be holy, (v.25) i.e. with the holy, O my Lord, thou wilt make thyself holy, giving to him that holiness of which a grant has been made, in order that, having become perfect in it, thou make him enter the fitting reward, and the rest (of) these (words) are in the (same) connection. And with the froward thou wilt pervert, (v.26) i.e. he did not say: with the froward thou wilt be perverse, (but) thou wilt pervert. For God, hindering the course to
deceit, diverts him that runs to evil things, blocking his evil way and setting aside his will in order that, being bound, he may desist from the evil that was planned; and he does not say: he makes him froward. Again: with the froward, thou wilt be perverse, i.e. in order that he might draw the evil ones to good and overcome the evil ones with good. Thou wilt light my lamp, (v.28) i.e. God is light and he enlightens that mind which he called a lamp. The part of the soul which receives light is the mind, that is to say, reason is called a lamp. It is not a light in its essence, but it is its receptable. Darkness of this part is anger and desire. When thus the mind is enlightened by the Lord, then also the irrational emotions of the soul are enlightened. In God (I) pass over a wall, (v.29) i.e. a wall he names the multitude of afflictions. My God, whose way is blameless, (v.30) i.e. not like the defiled ways of the gods of the heathen that are full of adultery and murder. The way of the Lord is excellence, walking in which we attain to him, and he again is the way and in him we proceed to the father. The oracles of the Lord are tried, (v.30) i.e. because there is no deceit in them and they are a fire that burns and consumes the strawiness of the passions. He made my feet like (the feet) of a hind, (v.33) i.e. for the hinds are the killers of snakes; pursued by hunters, they escape to the mountains. As the mountains are for the hinds,
so also the excellent when they are pursued by Satan, leave their earthly works at once and go up to the mountains, i.e. to excellence, and direct the course of their lives to holiness. Like a bow of brass he made my arms, (v.34) i.e. brass he calls the strength. And he teaches my hands war, (v.34) i.e. hands he calls the practical operations of the soul by which it is released for this, as it were; arm (he calls) the power and strength of the soul. Again when (he says) bronze, on the one hand, he refers to the impenetrability and strength; by the bow, on the other hand, he refers to this that arrows will be discharged by our arms, which are able to pierce those who oppose us. Thy right hand will sustain me, (v.35) i.e. the right hand of the father is the son and he who, having come down to us, helped and strengthened and guided and saved. Thy instruction will educate me, (v.35) i.e. the gospel teaching. Thou hast made my steps wide, (v.36) i.e. the Messiah enlarged our steps, the walking in excellence, adding the law of the gospel by which our footsteps are established which formerly were weak in the law book. I will pursue my enemies, (v.37) i.e. for having received help from God and widening of the steps and firm footsteps that he might pursue the enemies; the end of the pursuit is the extinction of the enemies. I shall smite them and they shall not be able to stand, (v.38) i.e. he will smite lying,
i.e. he will suppress (it) thereby that he will not swear at all; drunkenness(he will smite) by drinking water; slander, thereby that he will bless everyone; deception, thereby that he will not speak at all; then the spiritual enemies will not be able, to stand, but they will fall under our feet. They will fall beneath my feet, (v.38) i.e. the falling of the demons under the feet of the saints is their subjugation and overthrow. And my enemies he has crushed before me, (v.40) i.e. he refers to the complete victory that was given us by God over the demons. They will cry out, but they will not have a savior, (v.41) i.e. the heathen cried out to the idols, but the work of their hands did not save them. They will beseech the Lord, but he will not answer them, (v.41) i.e. he refers to the demons, as Isaiah said: if you multiply prayers, I will not hear you. Your hands are full of blood-how so? Because of the son they said: his blood be upon us. Beat them into pieces like dust, (v.42) i.e. the heretics that make a plea for error were like chaff before the wind; they were trampled upon like clay and this of the streets where they are many that trample; it is an ordinary thing that there are a multitude in the streets that trample. Observe how man shatters the enemies like chaff before the wind.
Again consider how worldly wisdom of the wicked and their riches and their glory and their short lives are not different from that chaff which is blown up from the earth and scattered. Save me from the gainsayings of the people, (v.43) i.e. the son, having been made man, said to the father: save me from the stiff-neckedness and the insubordination of the people. Thou wilt make me the head among the gentiles, (v.43) i.e. thou wilt appoint me the head of the church of the gentiles. Again thou wilt appoint me chief and foremost. By the word head he indicates the foremost. David was not king over the gentiles, but the Messiah, and therefore they refer to him. A nation that I did not know, (v.43) i.e. this that he says he did not know does not denote that it is ignorance, but that these which at some time were not of thy household were brought into subjection in my yoke, and those nations know me that did not know me through the law and the prophets, and afterwards they learned to know me. With the hearing of the ears they shall hearken to me, (v.44) i.e. for although everyone hears with the ear, yet he hears with a human and mortal hearing; he that hearkens to God, hears with a divine ear. Strange sons deceived me, (v.45) i.e. he calls them strange sons because by lineage from Abraham they descend; strange (he calls them) because of their manner, i.e. their evil way of living. Strange sons grew old and staggered off (the paths), (v.45) i.e. again he names the people
sons who, sinning and repenting not, grow old in evil, with excellence they are not rejuvenated. They staggered from (the paths), (v.45) i.e. the Jews erred and they did not want to walk in the way that was shown them by the law. The Lord liveth and blesseth, (v.46) i.e. the host of the apostles is saying: although the Lord suffered in the flesh, yet he lives and this that he lives is not as receiving life, for he is the giver of life. In essence the son is equal with the father; as the father is said to live, so also the son is said again to be blessing because every blessing belongs to him and he blesses the saints. May the God of my salvation be exalted, (v.46) i.e. because the Jews called him dead who was crucified, the prophet called out: the Lord lives and blessed be my God and may God be exalted, i.e. for not only does he live, but he also ascended to heaven and gives salvation to those who seek (it). Again he even humbled himself, bending down the heaven and coming down, but he is exalted, as (we read): God has greatly exalted him. Again God (is exalted) not as ascending to an exalted position, but when we in our praise confess: we exalt him with our thoughts, God who gave me vengeance, (v.47) i.e. on the devil. The apostles were the ones who subjugated the gentiles and took vengeance on the demons who had led astray the gentiles. They subjugated the gentiles, (v.47) i.e. the nations which were
brought into subjection by the apostles. From those that stand against me, lift me up, (v.48) i.e. from the chiefs of the Jews. Save me from the wicked man, (v.48) i.e. Judas, the betrayer, for he acted wickedly against him who had crowned him with apostleship. Therefore I will praise thee, (v.49) i.e. the host of the apostles says these (words) because of the multitude of the gentiles that entered the gospel. He increased the deliverance of his king, (v.50) i.e. the son he calls the king, not in as much as he is king over his father, but because he is given authority over everything like his father, and as he is his son, so also he is his king, and to the sonship of God by nature also the rank of kingship is joined. Again the father increased the salvation of his king, the Messiah, through those which he gave to be saved by him. He shows mercy to his anointed, (v.50) i.e. he showed mercy to his anointed, having pity upon those that were under the anointed in whose behalf he acts as priest and over whom he is king. For the word and term anointed denotes a priest and king, for mercies (done) to us are reckoned to the Messiah in as much as he is the head of our body. He showeth kindness to his anointed David, (v.50) i.e. these (words) refer to the Messiah to whom there was eternal praise at the end of time because he was made flesh. It is said that he received them and gave them to us. He was anointed with the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Psalm according to the Peshitta: it refers to the descent and the ascension in the flesh of our Lord and (his) battle with the demons and the death and the quakes
that took place at the crucifixion and the rejection of Israel and the calling of the gentiles. It was spoken by David at the time when the last Philistine was killed who is a type of the devil who was vanquished by Immanuel. I will love thee, O Lord, my strength, (v.1) i.e. because of many things it is fitting for thee that I love thee because thou hast created, saved and visited me. The pangs of death and sheol, (v.4,5) i.e. of death, and that means that he humiliated himself to the death of the cross. And the torrents of ungodly men, (v.4) i.e. the Jews. He heard from his temple, (v.6) i.e. from heaven, i.e. because he arose from death and was freed from the gloomy pangs of sheol. And the earth was troubled and it trembled, (v.7) i.e. there being darkness at the crucifixion. The foundations of the mountains trembled, (v.7) i.e. the rocks that were rent; again the evil thoughts of the Jews. Because thou was angry with them, (v.7) i.e. he destroyed them by death and took their captivity captive, he delivered many of them to torment. There went up smoke in his anger, (v.8) i.e. the darkness which was at the crucifixion he calls smoke, or because having extinguished the demonical fire which was inflaming men, smoke was coming forth, or again because the father was angry at the Jews and set their temple afire, then as Isaiah taught and said: the house was filled with smoke. Fire from his face was kindled, (v.8) i.e. the divine fire of the Messiah, kindled by the crucifixion, extinguished the fire of the demons. Coals burned by it, (v.8)
i.e. the spiritual powers of the demons burned and were overcome by the crucifixion, because he desired to show that he who did these (things) was the Lord and not an ordinary man; as if he received good tidings, he sang. He bent down the heavens and came down, (v.9) i.e. God himself and the son who was obedient unto a death of this sort. He bent down, i.e. the exaltedness of the hidden nature of his deity, and he humbled himself, came down, took lodging in a virgin and appeared in the flesh. Darkness was under his feet, (v.9) i.e. darkness he calls the inscrutability of the way of his providence which is hidden from all the world and from the multitude of angels and demons until his ascension. And he rode upon cherubs and flew, (v.10) i.e. as the Book of Acts teaches: a cloud received him and he was hidden from their eyes and entered his hidden nature. He made darkness his secret place, (v.11) i.e. darkness he calls his incomprehensibility and inscrutability. For although he appeared in the flesh, yet he is hidden and invisible in his deity. Again darkness he calls his invisibility and his mode of being with us at present, as (we read) behold I am with you until the end. Around him is his tabernacle, (v.11) i.e. in the Greek: lodging place, the holy church which is round about him and in which he has promised to abide, as (it is written): where two or three are gathered together, there am I in the midst of them. The darkness of the waters in the clouds (of the air) (v.11) i.e. waters he here calls the words of prophecy which were spoken obscurely
concerning him; clouds he calls the angels because also between him and them is darkness, i.e. incomprehensibility and hidden nature. His clouds he made hail and coals, (v.12) i.e. these are spoken prophetically because of the trials and persecutions and the captivity that befell the Jews after his ascension and again the freeing of the world from the demons which were driven away by the apostles whom he calls clouds which poured down rain upon the demons. Hail and coals of fire (v.13), he sent his arrows, (v.14) i.e. the apostles are coals and hail and arrows by which the demons are pierced, and he enlightens the habitable earth. The fountains of water appeared, (v.15) i.e. the teachings of the gospel, being revealed, became the foundations of the world and upon them we are built a holy building. At thy rebuke and thy breath, (v.15) i.e. by thy commands and thy will the spiritual enemies are overthrown. He sent from above and drew me out, (v.16) i.e. the human nature from sin. And he took me from the waters, (v.16) i.e. he drew me out of trials. Strong enemies, (v.17) i.e. the demons and death. They came upon me in the day of my affliction, (v.18) i.e. and the rest of the sentence, the prophet taking on the person of the human nature, are spoken thus. The Lord awarded me according to my righteousness and the cleanness, (v.20) i.e. they are spoken personifying those just ones that were waiting for the salvation of Israel and
the salvation of the world. With the holy thou wilt be holy, (v.25) i.e. by these (words) he makes known to all that every one he rewards according to his deeds. Because thou (wilt save) the needy people, (v.27) i.e. that of the apostles and the believers. Proud eyes (thou wilt bring down), (v.27) i.e. of the scribes and Pharisees. Thou wilt light my candle, (v.28) i.e. my mind. He will light my darkness; ignorance, sin, trials and death he calls darkness which came upon us, and he desires that we be freed of them. By thee I will run upon a troop, (v.29) i.e. the spiritual enemies. By thee I will leap over a wall, (v.29) i.e. the building which sin built against us. In thee we will begin a blameless way (of life). The oracle of the Lord (is pure), (v.30) i.e. the gospel. He is a helper to all who trust (in him) (v.30) i.e. to all who believe because they have passed from death to life, and this is so because God is the Lord and not a common and deceiving human being, according to the idle talk of the Jews and the Nestorians, and this is so because there is no God but the Lord. God who has girded me with strength, (v.33) i.e. he girded the apostles, as (we read): until ye shall be endured with power from on high. He made my feet like (the feet) of a hind, (v.33) i.e. that we might trample under foot the serpents and the scorpions as he, being incarnated, trampled under foot the entire hostile host, and he is called a hind in the Song of Songs. And on high he placed me, (v.33) i.e. he brought me back to the place from which Adam had fallen which is paradise. He taught my hands war, (v.34) i.e. spiritual (war) against the demons.
He has made firm like a bow of brass (my arms), (v.34) i.e. the angelic host that accompanies those that go to battle. Thou hast given me the shield (of thy salvation), (v.35) i.e. that faith regarding which Paul says: take the shield of faith with which you are able to quench the darts of the evil ones. Thou has made my steps wide (under me) that (my ankles) might not be moved, (v.36) i.e. thou hast placed my feet upon the rock of faith that I might not be moved by ferocious trials, but might pursue and overtake them. Thou wilt gird me with strength, (v.39) i.e. because I desire to conquer and it is not pleasant for me to fall under them, thou art sending strength to my aid. I will beat them to pieces like the dust before (the wind), (v.42) i.e. as dust does not remain before a strong wind, so they also are not able to withstand me. Thou wilt deliver me from the strivings of the people, (v.43) i.e. the scribes and Pharisees. Thou wilt make me the head of the gentiles, (v.43) i.e. because the Jews did not believe, the apostles turned and made disciples and became the heads to the gentiles. Strange sons, (v.44) i.e. he calls the gentiles because they were not the sons of God like Israel. They shall fade away and stagger from the paths, (v.46) i.e. from every kind of sinful path.

The 19 Psalm. In this psalm he makes known the manifestation of the Messiah, and it is spoken as if in the person of the apostles to the gentiles, and because the gentiles believed that the luminaries were gods, he mentions that the heavens and the luminaries are creatures, offering up praise to their maker. The heavens declare the praise (of God), (v.1) i.e. the heavenly hosts.
The firmament shows the work of his hands, (v.1) i.e. the firmament, while incapable of rational speech, shows by its circuit and its movement that it is a creature, as (we read): the hidden things of God by his works are clearly seen. Day unto day (uttereth speech), (v.1) i.e. by means of the movement of the luminaries by which the days and the nights and the seasons of the year are known; while they do not have reason and mind and hearing and voice, (yet) they proclaim that they have a creator, as a ship that is well proportioned proclaims that it has a maker. In all the land there is gone out (their tidings), (v.4) i.e. all the world, seeing the luminaries, marvels at the rational wisdom (displayed) in them. Like the sun he pitched (his tent), (v.4) i.e. in the firmament. And he (rejoices) like a bridegroom, (v.5) i.e. the sun; the bridal-chamber is this world. The law of the Lord, and so forth, (v.7) i.e. such is the nature of the creation that from its orderliness it is known that there is a God. A different (way): In all the earth there is gone out their tidings, (v.4) i.e. the gospel of the apostles. And upon the sun, (v.4) i.e. the Messiah is the sun of righteousness who made his tabernacle, that is to say, his church through the apostles a bridal chamber, shining forth first from sheol; again shining from Golgotha upon the gentiles, dark in sin, and enlightening them through the twelve apostles as in twelve hours. He exults like a hero, (v.5) i.e. because he vanquished death and the devil. Upon the ends of the heavens, (v.6) i.e. to all the
world he shone, going forth and enlightening everyone, the spiritual congregations of the souls as well as of the angels. Nothing is hid from his heat, (v.6) i.e. of the fire that he cast in the earth, of love, of keeping of commandments, of the gift of the spirit. The law of the Lord is without blemish, (v.7) i.e. the law and the testimony of the gospel with which the son testifies of himself: everyone who believes in me, rivers, (etc) and I am gone out from the father, etc. And making wise the babes, (v.7) i.e. either the simple in knowledge or the innocent with respect to evil. The commands of the Lord, (v.8) the gospel (commands). Pure and enlightening the eyes, (v.8) i.e. for the spiritual eyes of the mind and not for the body alone the commands are enacted like those of Moses. The judgments of the Lord are in justice, (v.9) i.e. because he judges the devil as (we read): now is the judgment of this world. More to be desired than gold, (v.10) i.e. and this (is thus) because of the reward for the sake of them, which is something that eye has not seen, etc. Who can perceive the slippery places? (v.12) because prophecy knows the slippery places in sin which cause us to go astray from the commandments, therefore the prophet asks that he be delivered from such as those. And from (hidden) sins cleanse me, (v.12) i.e. from the lurking places of the snares of the demons. Not shall evil ones be given authority over me,
(v.13) i.e. the demons. I shall be cleansed of my sins, (v.13) i.e. he asks that he be cleansed by repentance from his sins. Concerning the same psalm according to the LXX: rightly this psalm is superscribed by In the end; it makes known the appearance of the Messiah. For at the end of the age the multitude of types that are in it were fulfilled. The heavens declare his praise, (v.1) i.e. the heavens do not pronounce his praise but by means of their spectacle they incite others to a song of praise. The trees offer up praise and this indeed (they do when) they cause praise to ascend to him that created them. And the heavens and the earth and the trees are said to offer up a song of praise when others because of them praise. Therefore by (their) spectacle they cause admiration; so also those that lead an ascetic life in excellence, although they remain silent, they praise God, others because of them praising God. (The firmament) shows his handiwork, (v.1) i.e. because they are wondrously made, they proclaim the praise of God. The heavens are called the apostles in as much as they ponder on heavenly things. They do not proclaim through words, but through the signs which they do. The firmament shows, (v.1) i.e. the firmament is faith, for this strengthens our thoughts which were weak, through the beauty of worship. Day unto day uttereth, (v.2) the day of resurrection uttered to the day of crucifixion the word how he who on that (day) arose like God and raised the dead. Night unto night showeth (knowledge), (v.2) i.e. the night which was before the crucifixion spoke to the night of the betrayal of the Messiah
knowledge of this sort, how he who was terrified in that (night) prayed, and later was betrayed in this (night), is the Lord of the elements; how also it appeared that night in midday came to be. Again, night unto night, i.e. they teach how in the winter they are long and in the summers they are short. In all the land (there is gone out), (v.4) i.e. the wonderfulness of existing things and the discourses and the words concerning them are known to all men. And in the ends of the world, (v.4) i.e. words are in the world; in the soul which is more perfect and which was the habitation of God, are the complete and perfect doctrines. The sun which he made his tabernacle, (v.4) i.e. the Messiah is the sun in the flesh, that is to say, his tabernacle. Again he calls the sun his body because of its splendor and because it was free from sin and because, for a short time, as the sun, he dipped down from us to sheol giving light to those those buried. The sun he made his tabernacle, (v.4) i.e. he does not transgress the limit which the creator set for him, when as from the bridal chamber, as it is decreed for him, he goes forth, adorned as a bride-groom and resplendent with blossoming light, and he runs also the circuit like a strong hero from the border of the east and in one night and day he passes over the entire world and everyone feels his heat. Like a bridegroom
that goes forth, (v.5) i.e. the bridegroom is the Messiah who went forth from a virgin as from a pure bridal-chamber. He exults like a hero, (v.5) i.e. understand the incarnation in which he like a hero was exultingly running because of the power that was mustered at the crucifixion and death. The kampton is the turning place, that is to say, the place from which a man doubles upon himself to come to the place from which he began to run. The center is the middle of the circle. From the ends of the heavens is his going-forth, (v.6) i.e. in addition to this that like a bridegroom he went forth, in a carnal way from the bridal-chamber, that is to say, the virgin, he says that from the ends of the heavens he makes his going-forth, that is to say, from the bosom of the father. And his goal is the end of the heavens. (v.6) i.e. this one who went forth, that is to say, was born of the father, arrived at the end of heavens, ascending whence he had come of yore, to wit, if you will see the son of man who goes up thither where he had been before. Nothing is hid from his heat, (v.6) i.e. from his warmth no one is able to hide, for in that fire which he came to pour into the earth, everyone will share in order that men may become fervent in the spirit. Again as the blind, although they do not see the light of the sun, yet are partakers of its warmth, so also the unbe-
lievers, although they deny the deity of the Messiah, yet learn the power of his name, and also in the second advent no one will be hid from his heat when he comes openly and the fire is kindled before him, and he tries the deed of everyone. The law of the Lord is without blemish, (v.7) i.e. the law and the testimonies and the justice(s) and the commands and the judgments he calls the law of Moses; thus he ascribes the law to himself. He says at one time: the justice(s) and the commands which the Lord gave to Moses, and in another place: thou shalt keep the law of the Lord, thy God. And law it is called in as much as it lays out and determines the excellent way (of life); testimony, in as much as it testifies against those that sin and shows (their) punishment; justice(s) (it is called) in as much as it teaches justice and prevents iniquity shows as the righteous ones those who conduct their lives uprightly; commands, in as much as it commands that which is meet to do, and he commanded authoritatively; judgment, in as much as it shows what the divine decrees are: what rewards, on the one hand, he receives who keeps (the law), and to what punishment he is delivered who transgresses (it). The commands of the Lord are upright, (v.8) i.e. there is nothing perverse in them, but they perfect them who conduct their lives uprightly. The command of the Lord is choice and it enlightens, (v.8) i.e. what is more illuminating than this:
thou shalt not kill and not steal and not commit fornication? Those things which are called commandments more particularly and that enlighten the eyes of those who teach. The fear of the Lord is pure, (v.9) i.e. everything is known by its effects: fire from the fact that it warms, is said to be warm; the sun, from the fact that it illumens. Thus also the fear of the Lord is pure because it is an incitement to purity and lasts forever. The judgments of the Lord are in truth, (v.9) i.e. the judgments of the Lord are faithful; the judgments of lying and wicked judges are called true, but the faithful judges are just. Again, the judgments of the Lord he calls the divine laws and words because they were written in justice and with exact judgment. And they are sweeter than honey, (v.10) honey, which is perceptible to the senses, pleases the body; the divine law brings pleasure to the mind and the heart. Thy servant is warned by them-thy servant also keeps them, (v.11) i.e. he did not say this regarding himself alone, but regarding every servant of God. Thereby that one keeps them, is a great reward, (v.11) i.e. because by keeping them a heavenly reward comes to us, therefore we shall gather that which is great. Errors- who can understand (them), (v.12) i.e. manifest sins everyone knows, errors which are in secret, are those that are in thoughts; those that know them are rare, for this (we read): who makes known the trifles? Cleanse me
from the secret ones, (v.12) i.e. the sins that are not known to us he calls secret ones. Again, there are secret sins in the heart when there is robbery or adultery in the thoughts, or when we scheme to do evil to the enemies. Cleanse me, (v.12) i.e. make me free. Also withhold thy servant from iniquity, (v.13) LXX: have pity on thy servant from strange (sins) i.e. of strange sins; when the teacher neglects the pupils and the father the children or the priest the people, these are punished in the place of the hearers in as much as they neglected them and were the cause of the sin. Again strange (sins) he calls pride and fraud and greed and rage and anger; these passions are foreign things that are poured out upon the mind because they are of Satan and it is meet that as foreign ones we cut them off from us. Unless (evils) rule over me - then shall I be blameless, (v.13) how should not rule over us the sins of the brethren when we are not mindful of their affairs, or by carelessness or by (being) the cause of evil; we ought rather to be an example to them of good, in conduct as well as in speech. And I shall be innocent of great sin, (v.14) he says at the end; if namely I am innocent of my secret (sins); when these sins remain, they lead into a deceitful manner of living and then I am overcome of great sin. May the words of my mouth be pleasing, (v.14) i.e. when I pray and praise, those words of mine are pleasing that
are worthy of acceptance. The meditation of my heart, (v.14) i.e. the psalm he calls the meditation of the heart. Is meet for the mind to be directed to God in prayer and not to send forth words by means of the lips, the heart being in a different place.

The 20 Psalm. May the Lord hear thee in the day of affliction, (v.1) i.e. the psalm is spoken personifying his companions who were praying for him. Others say that David spoke it when he prayed for Solomon. Help from his sanctuary, (v.2) i.e. from heaven. And from Zion, (v.2) i.e. from the spiritual (Zion). Then we will praise thy salvation, (v.5) i.e. we or the companions of David. The psalm is understood concerning Solomon and personifying the apostles as if (spoken) on the day of crucifixion. Thy salvation (we will praise), (y.5) i.e. that (slavation) by which thou hast saved the world by the incarnation of thy Only (Begotten) and by his resurrection. May the Lord fulfill thy every desire, (v.5) i.e. that in which thou hast prayed that thou mayest save the world (and) that in which thou hast asked that thy disciples may be kept. It is known that God saved his anointed, (v.6) i.e. that people of the nations which thou hast anointed for a priestly kingdom. Again the Messiah was heard when he prayed for all the world. It is said that the Messiah was saved when salvation came to those who are his body and his members. And in regard to the words it is
known, (v.6) i.e. in this world we know that the anointed, our race, was saved; do not draw near to my anointed ones, and Saul was called the anointed. He answered him from the heaven of his holiness, (v.6) i.e. the father (answered) him by whom he saved the worlds. And the salvation of his right hand, (v.6) he calls the Messiah the right hand. Some in chariots (grow strong), i.e. the demons, the Jews, and those of the house of Pilate and Herod. But we in his name, (v.6) the apostles who were saved from those who were enemies, believing in the name of Jesus, the Nazerene. Concerning the same (psalm) according to the LXX. May the Lord hear thee in the day of affliction, (v.1) i.e. at all times the attention of the saints is directed to God and from him they ask help. May the Lord hear thee, (v.1) i.e. David was praying that he might find God, the Savior, while fighting with the enemies; with David either the host of angels or the order of priests were praying, and these were saying: may the Lord hear thee in the time of affliction, etc. May he send help to thee from his sanctuary, (v.2) i.e. from the holy one may help be sent to thee. Again he did not say: may help be sent to thee by riches or from men, but from the holy one, i.e. from holiness. And from Zion may he succour thee, (v.2) i.e. because from there the Savior shone forth to men. Again because before Zion he bestowed peace upon his apostles.
May he remember thy every sacrifice, (v.3) i.e. a sacrifice is different from a whole burnt offering; the term sacrifice is used concerning inanimate things, that are offering for a burnt offering; a whole burnt offering is a sacrifice of animate things. May the Lord give thee according to thy heart, (v.4) i.e. this was not said concerning every man, for a man does not say this concerning a lover of adultery and thievery, but it is fitting for the saints because they have a good heart and a mind that is correct and a meditation that is directed to God. Again God gives according to the heart of him who prays, when he asks those things which are proper for God to give. For the heart of the Christians is answered in those things that God wants and these it asks. We will rejoice in thy salvation, (v.5) i.e. salvation is the Messiah; there is born to you a Savior, the Lord Christ. And in the name of the Lord we will become great, (v.7) i.e. some magnify themselves with wealth, others with vain praise; the saints, however, are great and boast in God. May he fulfill all thy petitions, (v.5) i.e. what is the petition? Holy father, keep them in thy name. Again fulfillment (of) prayer goes into effect when he prays something with which God is pleased. Answer him from the heaven of his holiness, (v.6) i.e.
when the Messiah ascended into heaven, he opened heaven for men, answering from there our prayers from here. The Jews, on the one hand, he was answering from one place, the temple; this, then, Solomon prayed when he founded the temple. Us, on the other hand, he answers from all the heaven, a wide and great altar. With power and the salvation of his right hand, (v.6) i.e. the right hand of the father is the Messiah, not as if he were a member or a part; undivided, namely, is God and without form- but as the might and power. Salvation is that which the Messiah accomplished by his heroism in the crucifixion and death. For by these he vanquished the strength of the enemies. Some in chariots and some in horses, (v.7) i.e. as he drowned the chariots and horses of the Egyptians when he saved Israel, so also, saving our race, did he shatter the chariots of the demons. Again, horses, he calls those who are drawn after passions upon which the hosts of the demons ride. Chariots he names the gatherings together of heathen passions by which the demons fight against us. As for us, our battle is valiant which is an appellation of God. Again horse he calls one of the passions that dwells in us upon which the demons ride (and) concerning which Moses said: the horse and his rider he cast into the sea. Chariots (he calls the multitude of passions that are combined, as riches with boasting and vain glory. Lord, save the king and answer us, (v.9) i.e. king he calls the mind which is in the image of God, for when this is saved and vigilant, it is answered,
whenever it cries to God.

The 21 Psalm. According to Daniel and Zëura and Athanasius. The companions of the kind are also singing this psalm, in as much as David was gladdened because the Messiah was to arise from his seed in the flesh. Thou settest on his head, (v.3) i.e. the crown he calls the nations because like a crown he surrounded him with nations. Thy right hand shall find, (v.8) i.e. the Jews and the demons. In the time of anger, (v.9) i.e. torment. And they are not able, (v.12) i.e. to destroy the Messiah by the cross because he arose and put them to shame. Be thou exalted, O Lord, (v.13) i.e. when he ascended to heaven. Another: May the king rejoice in thy power, O Lord, (v.1) i.e. the king is the mind in us which was created in the image of God. In thee, namely, it will rejoice and not in earthly things. Thou gavest (him) the desire of his heart, (v.2) i.e. because thou hadst desired to be incarnated and to save him and to bring back the primaeval incorruptibility in paradise. Because thou anticipatest him with a good blessing, (v.3) i.e. that first blessing when thou didst create him, thou didst say: be fruitful and multiply. Thou hast placed a crown on his head, (v.3) i.e. thereby that thou hast made him king and head of those creatures (that are) apprehended by the senses, and because thou hast finally saved him when he had sinned. Life he
asked of thee and thou gavest him, (v.4) i.e. and first of all, because the mind is not subject to dissolution like the body; secondly, life which is in faith and knowledge. Great was his honor. Praise and splendor thou heapest upon him, (v.5) i.e. immortality and incorruptibility with which thou didst endow him when thou wast incarnated and didst receive flesh, endowed with soul and mind, and didst join it to thee. And he was great and honored in thy salvation, (v.5) i.e. because thou hast liberated him from the curse of the transgression of the commandment, and so thou hast made him a blessing (v.6). By the mercy of the most high, (v.7) i.e. because the king believed in thee and trusted in thee, that is to say, the mind shall not be moved by the onrushing billows of sin. Thy hand shall find, etc. (v.8) i.e. nay, he will rebuke those that hate him and will vanquish them by his right hand. The time of anger, (v.9) i.e. of judgment. Fire shall consume them, (v.9) i.e. that (fire) which is prepared for the devil and his angels. His fruit (he will destroy) from the earth, (v.10) i.e. the evil seeds that he sows into the human heart, and these (things happen) because they intended evil against me, (v.11) i.e. they cast me out of paradise and caused me to transgress the commandments. They devised a plan, but not... (v.11) i.e. the plan that they devised was that when we cast ourselves down, we should perish, but they did not prevail because God did not deliver us up, but freed us and saved us and raised us up. Thou wilt place a mark on them, (v.12) i.e. the everlasting fire. Be thou exalted in
thy might, O Lord, (v.13) i.e. when thou humblest them, then wilt be exalted by the saints. We will sing and praise, (v.13) i.e. we will exult and rejoice in the salvation. Concerning the same (psalm) according to the LXX. This hymn David spoke when he vanquished the Philistine and rejoiced and danced. Thus also the new people rejoices and exults in the Messiah. Thou hast given him the desire of his heart, (v.2) i.e. he who does not follow the desire of the flesh, is made perfect in the spirit; and when he is imbued with the spirit, he receives the desire of his heart from God since he is filled with good for his desire. The preparation of his lips, (v.3) i.e. the supplications and the mouth and the lips of David are the singers because they were singing his psalms; they were always asking David to prophesy psalms generously, as he was (doing), that is to say, that they might gather the great treasures of the psalms. Thou hast placed a crown of precious stone on his head, (v.3) i.e. they say concerning David that when he found a stone in the crown of Malcom, the idol of the Moabites and the Ammonites, he put it in his crown. Again a crown and precious stones are the Messiah. For by him we are crowned and blessed. Again, a crown is the circlet of the commandments. For the commandments hang together in the manner of a crown, whose writing, on the one hand, is set in the guise of gold; the spirit, on the other hand, shines forth preeminently as a precious stone. He asked life of thee and thou gavest, (v.4) i.e. he points forward to the resurrection and the endless life. The man that is in the Messiah does not ask anything among the temporal things, but the life to come.
And prolongation of days, (v.4) i.e. with life he asks length of days in order that deathlessly and without end he may receive length of days. Great was his praise in thy salvation, (v.5) i.e. although dishonor we were bringing because of sin, the salvation of the Messiah exalted us above the heaven and the angels. Praise and splendor, (v.5) i.e. praise and confession he calls the deity of the Messiah which Ezekiel spoke praising: blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place, (i.e.) the place of God; everything in every place the prophet proclaimed for the praise of God. Because thou hast made him a blessing, (v.6) i.e. the blessing of the Jews was temporal; therefore also from the earthly Mount Gerizim it was given. Then the (blessing) of the church is from heaven forever. Thou hast made him glad with the gladness of thy countenance, (v.6) i.e. the countenance of the father is the son; he that sees me sees my father. With him we will be delighted in heaven just as the friends of the bridegroom with the bridegroom. Because the king trusts in the Lord, (v.7) i.e. he that trusts in the Lord is rightly called king because every creature is subservient to him; therefore we will also trust in God that we may also reign with him. In the goodness of the Highest he will not be moved, (v.7) i.e. although we have many virtues, yet the goodness of the Lord and his mercies alone are able to establish us; it is not his therefore that desires nor his that runs, but God's who has mercy. Thy hand shall find
all thy enemies, (v.8) i.e. these words point forward to the Jews who devised evil things against our Savior. Again, his hand is capable of handling all the enemies of God, that is to say, it will bring punishment and wage war with them. For the Lord will wage war with Amalek with a hidden hand.
