Again, the hand and the right hand he calls the son, and the hand and the right hand are the same, as (we read): I will raise my hand against the heaven, and he swore by my right hand, that is to say, he swore therefore by the son who is equal to him in essence; it is not fitting that he sware by another who is greater than he, except by himself. Thou wilt make them like a furnace of fire at the time of anger, (v.9) i.e. of thy countenance; when the radiance of thy praise, that is to say, the image of thy face shall shine forth at the end of time, then they will burn as if in a furnace of fire with the torment which they shall kindle for them from the outside, they bring from the inside the fire to themselves. Also the Jews, being the murderers of their Lord, were kindled like a furnace of fire at the time of the countenance of the father and fire consumed them, that is to say, war and famines and flight and captivity and the sword. Lord, in thy anger thou wilt confound them, (v.9) i.e. for although God is a lover of mankind, yet, according to justice, he shows anger and wrath for the wicked from whom we pray to be delivered. Thou wilt destroy their fruit from the earth, (v.10) i.e. he will
not destroy their being, but those, who in an evil way have brought fruit, are evil gain and adulterous deeds. And their seed is from men, just as plants from that which is sown, bear seed and other plants sprout from them, so as also those who bear fruit in evil and wickedness scatter seeds of teaching in order to bring about deceitful ones and those evil in wickedness, who are like them. The seed of this God destroys from men. They intended evil against thee, (v.11) i.e. the Jews were inclined to evil and the enemies of our Savior came to light. They devised those plans that, (v.11) i.e. ailen is halen, which (are those which) it is written in the gospel, that they made against the Messiah. For they devised a plot which they were not able to carry out. because they hoped that into death they might cast down the Lord of glory. The plan of sinners are not able to stand because God stands who is against their (plan). Thou wilt put them back, (v.12) i.e. the Jews he calls back, because the first are the last. They were thrown backwards, i.e. back, and the heathen stood before them. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous; he sees fit to look upon the righteous. Again in flight, those who flee are accustomed to turn the back. The wicked flees when he is not pursued. In thy remnants thou wilt prepare their faces, (v.12) i.e. the remnants he calls those
of the Jews who were saved by repentance when they were not ashamed to draw near to the sinful (woman) and to the host which is saved. May the Lord be exalted in thy strength, (v.13) i.e. not (as) being needy, was God exalted, but having descended to our weakness and having been crucified because of weakness, he was exalted in his power. Show thy exaltedness through thy unspeakable power; we, praising thee, will sing and speak, relating thy wonders.

The 22 Psalm. Concerning the succour, by David. i.e. when from the gloom of the devil and the night of sin the Messiah freed us and arose in the dawn from the grave; hence it is entitled: of the dawn. The Messiah sings this psalm personifying humanity and he relates those things that happened to the Messiah at the time of the crucifixion. My God, my God, give attention to me; why hast thou forsaken me, (v.1) i.e. he asks therefore attention from the father, placing the things that are ours upon himself. We were continuing as the forsaken through the transgression of Adam until the time that he was incarnated and saved us. Thou hast removed from me my salvation by the words of my sins, (v.1) i.e. if he had not taken on human form, how would these be fitting for the son, because behold he did no sin and neither was deceit found in his mouth, as Isaiah says. My God, I cried unto thee day and night, (v.2) i.e. because he was incarnated, he offers up for us this petition and intercession.
or because the saints constantly are petitioning for that salvation which is through him. Thou art holy and dwellest in the glory, (v.2) i.e. in thee it is bound up and thou art the glory of Israel. My fathers trusted in thee, (v.3) i.e. the fathers in the flesh were Abraham and the rest of the just ones and the prophets. I namely am a worm, (v.5) i.e. although I am a worm, being incarnated in the likeness of human seed- that which fell into the womb, took on the likeness of a worm at first, then it grew and increased- yet I am not a man by nature, because I am not from a seed; yet man indeed I am, while I am God by nature. Again, as a worm is not of seed or of copulation, but of putrefaction so also the Word, God, since our nature is subject to putrefaction and corruptible, in part became a worm and a man that he might renew it and give to it life and incorruptibility. A reproach of men, etc. (v.6) i.e. at the time of the crucifixion he was reproached by the Jews: if thou art the son of God, come down from the cross; he trusted in God, let him come. Because thou art my trust from the womb and my hope, (v.9) i.e. because he was incarnated by the will of the father. Because affliction has drawn near, (v.11) i.e. of the people of the Jews. Oxen have surrounded me, (v.12) i.e. the priests and the teachers of the Jews. And the bulls of Basahn, (v.12) i.e. the peoples of Herod and Pilate, who were not harnessed under the yoke of Moses like the oxen. They opened their mouth against me, (v.13) i.e. they are changed from their nature and like lions and beasts they opened their mouth against me in their desire. And like water I am poured out, (v.14) i.e. because I am cast
forth into death. And my bones are scattered, (v.14) i.e. the apostles; for if the church is his body, then his bones and members are the disciples. The bones of his body were not scattered in the grave because he arose on the third day. And my heart was wax, (v.14) i.e. like liquified wax and this (was so) because he was grieved and distressed for the betrayer and for the Jews who were on the way to destruction because of the wickedness in them. My tongue cleaveth to my palate, (v.15) i.e. in the thirst which was on the cross when he said: I thirst, when they gave him myrrh to drink. And to the dust of death, (v.15) i.e. he tasted death in his goodness for everyone. Because dogs have surrounded me, (v.16) i.e. the chiefs of the Jews. They pierced my hands and my feet, (v.16) i.e. with nails. All my bones lamented, (v.17) i.e. from the nails and the blows. In the Greek: they counted all my bones, i.e. examining his body and measuring one by one of the bones to see where they ought to drive the nails. They gazed and gaped at me, (v.17) i.e. when they dressed me with a mantle and a crown of thorns and gave me a reed to hold. They divided my garments, (v.18) i.e. as (we read): the tunic was without seam and they cast lots over it. But thou, O Lord, do not withdrawn from me, (v.19) i.e. by these (words) he taught us and he was a type to us that we pray in trials. Deliver (my soul) from the sword,
(v.20) i.e. the spear that was thrust in his side. And from the hand of the dogs, (v.20) i.e. the Jews. From the mouth of the lion, (v.21) i.e. death and the devil. And from the horns, (v.21) i.e. the demons and the devil, and these words he prophesied of his suffering and death; then he turned to prophesy about his resurrection. Because I will declare thy name to my brethren, (v.22) i.e. these (took place) when he arose and his disciples saw him in Jerusalem and Galilee, as he had said: Go, say to my brethren; behold I will go before. They that fear the Lord, (v.23) i.e. the apostles and those that believed of the gentiles and became sons to Abraham. He hath not despised and not rejected the cry (of the needy), (v.24) i.e. when these believed in him, they learned that he did not despise the cry of Adam and of the human nature, but when it cried to him, he heard it and came down to it. Before thee (shall be) my praise, (v.25) i.e. not in the synagogue, but in the church; first, when the voice came: I have glorified and I will glorify; again, being glorified in sheol and being glorified in the visible church of the gentiles and in the spiritual church of the souls and in the assembly of angels. I will pay my vows before (them that fear him), (v.25) i.e. this (took place) when I became man and died and saved. Of them that fear the Lord, (v.25) i.e. then angels and the disciples and the preachers. The needy shall eat, (v.26) i.e. the gentiles were hungering for righteousness, ate the body and the blood, teaching (and) the way of life. He will let your heart live, (v.26) i.e. in faith all that go down
to the dust, the entire human nature, and also by the demons the lordship of the Messiah is confessed, and if here, (well and good; if not) then in the world to come when they shall be in torment and eat dust like the serpent whom they obeyed. My soul lives by him; in death my soul is alive in sheol, and in it, it proclaims and preaches him. The seed that will serve him will proclaim, (v.30) i.e. every believer who renders service to him and teaches and preaches and shows righteousness to the generation that come, i.e. those that were the first in the gospel, saw from the womb of baptism the Holy One and they show the righteousness of God forever. Concerning it according to the gathering of Andreas. Concerning the succour of the dawn, i.e. when the darkness of the devil had been spread over the world, there shone forth the only light of truth in our hearts and the ray of its knowledge gleamed into our souls. Again, it is called the succour of the dawn because our Lord arose from the grave in deep dawn, having trodden death under foot. My God, my God, give attention to me, (v.1) i.e. he was not forsaken by the father nor by his deity in as much as he feared the suffering. For who urged him to be born and later to ascend the cross? But we were those who were continuing as the forsaken through the transgression of the commandment of Adam, and as we were servants by nature and call God father, being honored with the rank of sons because the son became like us, so also (he who was) the son by nature, having become like unto us and having become man, called (him who was) his father by nature his God; and this word: give attention to me, and thou hast forsaken me, does not mean that he was outside
the person of the father. He asks namely the attention of the father for (the fact) that he had become man, bring up to him those (prayers) of ours. Why hast thou forsaken me, (v.1) i.e. that forsakenness might be removed, i.e. that these (things which come) from curses might be forsaken and that he might overcome death and might plant the root of incorruptibility. Far from my salvation are the words of my sins, (v.1) i.e. other translators wrote: words of my humble self, of my lamentations, of my crying, and not of my sins, for he did no sin: words of my lamentations, because of the people and my crying because of Judas. Far from my salvation are, (v.1) i.e. the people and the betrayer were not worth anything of the salvation which had been brought to them by me. Again because of us who had sinned and were in sins through the transgression of Adam, he said: far from, etc. and as he, being the fountain of blessings, took upon himself the sin and the curse that was upon us, so also in our stead (and) for our sakes he uses the words: far from my salvation in the words of my sins, i.e. do not look upon the sins of the nature, but give salvation because of my sufferings. My God, I will cry to thee by day and night, (v.2) i.e. not being in afflictions which are likened to the night, am I crying to thee that I might not suffer, but when bright (things prevailed), i.e. in the day, when I cried to thee, thou didst not answer, but didst surrender (me) to suffering. It is not according to my faulty reason. i.e. nay, however, I shall know the mystery of providence and I understand that thou dost not defer
the granting of prayer in vain. Again the day and the night he calls the time of the crucifixion, and it was from the sixth until the ninth hour. Then the Messiah cried for the Jews: Father, forgive them, and he did forgive; when they denied the resurrection, there was a return of sin upon them. In thee trusted my fathers, (v.3) i.e. although thou dwellest among the saints and hearest them, yet still more thou dwellest with thine Only One and hearest him. My fathers in the flesh trusted in thee, expecting my epiphany. In thee they trusted and not were they put to shame, (v.4) i.e. and not did they fall short of their hope. To thee they cried and they were saved, (v.4) i.e. they were delivered from death and the devil. Salvation by me and through me came to them, and these received (their) hope and expectation. They cried to thee, (v.4) i.e. when Pharaoh was pursuing them, they were terrified and cried to me, and presently they walked in the sea. I am a worm and not a man, (v.5) i.e. by this he teaches us humility. Again he shows clearly the lowest stage of his suffering and he alludes to the blotting out of the demons. When he was brought to death and when he was in sheol, he was about to deliver the hostile powers to corruption in the manner of a worm. Again he is named a worm and not a man because he did not receive birth in the flesh in the likeness of men through the intercourse of males and females. Therefore because he also partook of the power that was destructive of death, he is called a worm. Again he is not called a worm as denying his human nature, but to teach that he was not born by the law of cohabitation, and as a worm is not born of cohabitation but of the clay of the
earth, thus the Messiah was not born of cohabitation, but of a virgin and of the spirit, and he calls himself a worm, because he was clothed with flesh as a bait for the enemies with which he was hiding the fish-hook of his deity. A reproach of men and despised, (v.6) i.e. those who were mocking the Messiah, seeing him naked who was crowned with thorns and shaking their heads at him. Because thou art my hope from (the body), the LXX: because thou art he who has drawn me from the body, (v.9) i.e. he who is conceived by seed, is formed by a womb; our Savior, however, the father alone drew from the body of virginity, no seed having been cast into it, yet as from it he went forth, divine offspring. Upon thee have I been cast from the womb, (v.10) i.e. from the breasts, and the womb is mentioned because he was loved by the father since he became man, and it is known from this that he said to Joseph that he was to take the child and to flee from Herod, the murderer. From the body of my mother, thou art my God, (v.10) i.e. because he became man and went forth from a body; then he is also named God because he is the son of the father. Thou art my God, (v.10) Be not far from me, (v.11) i.e. these (words) which are fitting for providence, he speaks because he was man. Thereby (that he says): be not far from me, because there is no helper, he shows the anger of the Jews, and he teaches us to pray in trials. Many heifers have surrounded me, (v.12) i.e. fat ones. The heads of the Jews he calls oxen. Aquila: strong heifers of Basahn have encircled me, (v.12) i.e. the servants of
pilate who placed a crown of thorns on his head. They opened against me their mouth, (v.13) i.e. away with him, away with him; crucify him, crucify him. Like a roaring lion, (v.13) i.e. when a lion is hungry, he comes after an animal with a loud roar, and afterwards (also) when he is tearing it to pieces. Thus also the Jews roared against the Messiah saying: this one has said that he would tear down the temple. I am poured out like water, (v.14) i.e. water that is poured and dashed out goes to many places; thus when Jesus was taken, the disciples fled and were scattered like water. Again, water that is poured out on the earth, makes it bring forth fruits; thus also the suffering of the Messiah, when it was spread abroad, shows to all the world the bearing of fruits of the fear of God. All of my bones are scattered, (v.14) i.e. the apostles he calls (thus) because of (their) firmness and because they held together the body of the church. And my heart was like wax that is melted, (v.14) i.e. the distress and the anxiety that came to him in the flesh he alludes to; for if he bore our weakness, then the converse also is that he took upon himself distress. Again, doubtless it is my human heart which is melted like wax in the midst of the body, when it sees those that are born to suffer evil. Because the Messiah saw that the disciples were downcast and scattered, he lovingly gave attention to them. The suffering of wax he took upon himself in the midst of the body when he suffered with those (sufferings) of one giving birth. My strength is dried up like a pot-sherd, (v.15) i.e. he alludes to the thirst that befell him on the cross when he asked
to drink and they brought him vinegar. Dried up from thirst was his strength, naturally (that) in the flesh. Again, perhaps he calls Peter the strength of the Messiah when he confessed him that he was the son of God. He dried up in the denial and from then also he was prepared to be broken like a sherd, except that with tears he moistened himself, and he was prepared clay for a formation anew. My tongue cleaves to my throat, (v.15) i.e. because of the thirst when he asked to drink. To the dust of the earth thou hast brought me down, (v.15) i.e. by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone; for if he was born, he also died. The dust of death he calls the grave and sheol in which he was three days. Dogs have surrounded me, (v.16) i.e. the servants of Pilate who were not pure as idolators. And the gathering of the evil, (v.16) i.e. the people of the Jews and the heads of the murderous gathering. They pierce my hands and feet, (v.16) i.e. witness for this is that he answered: I have been lacerated, and the hands and the feet that were pierced. They count all my bones, (v.17) i.e. they examined his whole body and counted every one of the bones in order to know according to those (bones) how properly to drive the nails. Again, so they stretched me out, driving in nails, that it would be an easy (matter) for him who so desires, to know also the number of the bones. Again, the bones were the apostles; the flesh of the Messiah are those who believe in him correctly and literally.
Again, according to the number of the bones were the apostles and also the torments: they brought blows to the back, they bruised the head, they smote the cheeks, they gave the mouth vinegar to drink, they rived the side with a lance, they drove nails into the hands and feet. They watched and looked upon me, (v.17) i.e. this that they looked upon me was that they mocked and laughed. They know from the signs that they were sinning against God in what they did or prosecuted; when they sought sin in me, they found me sinless. They part my garments among themselves, (v.18) i.e. the gospel teaches this; literally concerning no other man did this happen in Israel. But thou, O Lord, be not far from me for my help, (v.19) i.e. the Messiah was not speaking these (words) for himself, but for humanity; rather also for himself, for these properties of mankind he took on because at one time he assumed that. Save (my soul) from the spear, (v.20) he calls death; he was not saying this because of his own soul, for he was alive; for us who are under death namely he was asking that we might be delivered from it. From the power of the dogs--my Only One, (v.20) i.e. dogs he calls the dominion of Satan. Again, dog he calls Satan because he rages impudently and fiercely against our souls. The Only One he calls the soul because there is nothing more precious to us than it which, it is meet, that we guard, as a man guards the only daughter because she more than all of the souls is subject to sin, and he is inseparably with her. Again, he names the Only One the church which exists with him and is perfect through the perfect ones (in it). Save me from
the mouth of the lion, (v.20) i.e. the gathering that cried out against him and accused him, he compares to the mouth of a lion. And from the horn of the unicorn, (v.21) i.e. from the arrogance of the heads. They say of the unicorn that it charges every animal and it is difficult to encounter because of the hardness and sharpness of its horn. I will declare thy name to my brethren, (v.22) i.e. brethren he calls the believers whom he taught to cry: our father in heaven. In the midst of the congregation I will praise thee, (v.23) i.e. of the gentiles. For in it he teaches that the father be praised; not therefore; he is praising, but the son makes known how it is meet that we praise the father. Ye who fear the Lord, praise him, (v.23) i.e. because for us there suffered he who is not subject to suffering. And all of the seed of Jacob praised him, (v.23) i.e. Jacob is name many sons. Sometimes in the Greek he explains Jacob as the son of Isaac; sometimes, the people from which he came forth; sometimes, the ten tribes that separated themselves and went out to Jeroboam; sometimes, the Messiah, as (we read): Jacob is my child; I will help him. He did not turn his face from me, (v.24) i.e. he does not turn his face from me, (v.24) i.e. not only that he does not turn from sinners, for from the face of all of them (he does not turn),
unless now the prophet were speaking; yet also when they cried to be delivered, quickly, he heard. From thee in my praise, (v.25) i.e. LXX: my praise; praise he calls praise-speaking, as I make thee known to men, so also thou teachest all men that they bring the same honor to me, when thou sayest: this is my beloved son, and at a time: I glorified and again I am glorified. The great congregation, (v.25) i.e. he names that one which comes to perfection. The needy shall eat, (v.26) i.e. the gentiles he calls the needy because they were lacking the blessings. Their heart shall live forever, (v.26) i.e. a mind which is cold through dead deeds, they have acquired; when they turn to God, they live, and he did not say: the bodies but the hearts in order that thou mayest learn that the nourishment of the heart and the soul is bread of the spirit. And before him all the tribes shall worship, (v.27) i.e. the Jews worshipped God in the temple; the gentiles, however, learned to worship in spirit and in truth; remaining where they were, they worshipped, since this is worshipping before God, whenever a man conducted himself as God desires, and with these (words) agrees Zephania, for he says: Everyone out of his place will worship him, all the islands of the gentiles. Because the kingdom is the Lord's, (v.28) i.e. the demons which previously were in possession, have been cast out, and the kingdom of God has taken hold. At first (the word) of prophecy says: they will call to remembrance, i.e. they will remember, and then: they will be converted, thirdly: they
will worship, and these (things) are (thus) because the kingdom is the Lord's, and he it is who is the ruler over the gentiles. They will eat and worship, (v.29) i.e. spiritual food, i.e. divine teaching, and when their mind is well nourished, they worship him. And before him, all those that go down to the dust shall bend the knee, (v.29) i.e. these that are earthly-minded whose downfall is of the judgment to come.

The 23 Psalm. A psalm of David concerning the shepherding of the Messiah and the calling of the gentiles and the delight in the sacramental meal. The Lord will shepherd me, (v.1) i.e. not an hireling or the prophet, but the Lord is a good shepherd. He will shepherd me, (v.1) i.e. a spiritual shepherd with whom there is no lack of sobriety nor of faith nor of material and spiritual delight. Upon meadows, (v.2) i.e. the prophetic and apostolic words. And to the quiet waters, (v.2) i.e. baptism and teaching, as (we read); everyone that believeth in me rivers.... He restored my soul, (v.3) i.e. from error and from death. In paths of justice, (v.3) i.e. in the evangelic commandments. Because of thy name, even though I walk, (v.3,4) i.e. since the human race had repented and believed and become strong in the keeping of the commandments, it does not fear death and the foes and the demons and the trials, and this is (this) that he fears no evil. Thy rod and thy staff, (v.4) i.e. rod and staff he calls the Messiah as (we read): a staff of strength the Lord will send thee from Zion. Again a rod and a staff are death and sheol which he ended and finished by becoming man. And they comfort me: from them flowed
to us the consolation of resurrection and of immortality which awaits us, death being abolished and sheol with it. Thou preparest before me a table, (v.5) i.e. the holy altars which are filled with the body and blood. Against my enemies, (v.5) i.e. the demons who are distressed because of the eucharist, and at table he says and not tables to point out that it is one and not many. Thou hast anointed my head with oil, (v.5) i.e. he points forward to the baptism, and the head he calls the mind and the oil (he calls) the chrism, i.e. the holy spirit. My cup satiates like unmixed (wine), (v.5) i.e. the sacramental cup of salvation, the spiritual cup of knowledge and excellence, as (we read): eat, my companions. Thy goodness and mercy follow me, (v.6) i.e. because we have been baptized and eaten and drunk of divine goodness, therefore from the running and the pursuit after goodness we will not cease, whether of our own accord or being pursued by goodness until we shall attain to the house of the Lord, (v.6) i.e. the Jerusalem above. Concerning it according to the LXX. The Lord will shepherd me, (v.1) i.e. for he that directs his life to humility and holiness was also called the sheep of the Messiah. He speaks of a good shepherd because namely the Lord is shepherding me. The pasture then is the evangelical teaching. He will make me lie down in a place of grass, (v.2) i.e. grass he calls the New Testament which never grows old. Water of rest, (v.2) i.e. quiet (waters), i.e. of
baptism through which we blot out our sins through which our race receives rest, putting from it the burden of sin. Because of the name, though I shall walk, (v.3,4) i.e. he saved us for the sake of his praise, we being unworthy of salvation, as he said: for thy name's sake forever. For even if I walk in the shadows of death, (v.4) i.e. if I should be in trials, I do not fear the evil of the demons, for there is a helper to thee. Again the shadows of death he calls the liberation of the soul from the body, because death of the soul, i.e. of sin, is not a shadow, but it is something real and the destruction of the soul. In the valleys of the shadows of death, (v.4) i.e. the shadows of death he calls those temptations which are death to sinners, for they are swallowed up by temptations. To the righteous therefore temptations are the shadow of death because they are not overcome by them. Thy rod and thy staff, they comfort me, (v.4) i.e. the Messiah is the staff and he is the comforter of those who lean upon him, because he does not forsake those that slip and descend to sin. Thy rod and thy staff, (v.4) i.e. staff he calls the admonition through counsel and exhortation; rod then (he calls) the severe chastisement as (we read): I shall come upon you with a rod. Again, if thou art a sinful sheep, with a rod thou art smitten, if, however, thou art a sinful man with a staff. Again, the word of God, which is comfort and exhortation to salvation to us, is a rod for the slothful; a staff, for the weak. Again, it typefies also the symbol of the cross, and of two staves, i.e. rods, is the cross composed. And a rod and staff the cross is called justly, and a staff, on the
one hand, for men is present, and a rod, on the other hand, for the demons. With a straight staff he supports and guides us who believe in him; he uses a rod with a line against the demons. Thou preparest before me a table against my oppressors, (v.5) i.e. he spoke of that sacramental supper which he prepared for us by means of his sacrifice. Against, (v.5) i.e. nothing is so averse to the demons as the sacramental table. My cup satiates as unmixed (wine), (v.5) i.e. it fillst with all blessings. As the best, i.e. the holder is firm because through it we receive power over the passions and the demons. And thy mercy shall follow me, (v.6) i.e. the mercy for mankind of God at all times cleaves to us, and we also hurt thy spirit, yet it follows the straying sheep like a shepherd.

div.head: THE LITERAL INTERPRETATION
div.ab:
A literal interpretation of the book of the Psalms. Now after we interpreted with the former work the Psalms of David in detail (and) more profusely, in this book, according to thy will, we are going to round it out briefly. And before we draw near to the enlightenment literally and spiritually, we decided that now we speak briefly concerning their literal sense and the occasions (at which they were spoken) and then in a second book after that variously therefore and copiously. Now with metre and sweet song David expounded his prophecy that he might attract the hearers to the love of his teaching, and whereas the end of the words of prose is not retained in the memory easily, those that are spoken in metre and song, are fixed firmly in mind. Further, the title and the occasions of the Psalms: after the return from Babylon they were set in order by an expert man, but not one after another in order did they write them, but in scattered fashion (and) according to their knowledge and pleasure; and it is known that the killing of Goliath comes before the persecution by Absolom and also the sin of Bathsheba. And in the third Psalm the persecution of his son is given as title which took place later, and in the fifty-first the sin of Bathsheba and in the one hundred and forty-third the killing of the Philistine, it would have been meet that it be placed first and then that of the persecution by Saul and gradually everyone in its time and order, which was not done. The first Psalm admonishes that we be pleasing to God in the fear of the Lord. The Hebrews take it concerning Joash because namely in the temple he meditated in the law before Jehoiada. Others say that Joash was a murderer and not worthy of the bless
ing. Blessed the man, (v.1) i.e. by one man he refers to many; because now difficult is the way of excellence, he sets forth as delightful the blessing, that on account of it we may despise the afflictions that come upon us. Way he calls the deeds; wicked (he calls) him that perverts his associate. Sinners he calls those that sin openly. Mockers (he calls) the ridiculers and the vain that ridicule the moral life of others. And council he calls the agreement of the will and standing according to the wicked and so forth. But in his law, (v.2) i.e. even though he refrains from evil, yet it behooves a man that he run toward good things. His foliage shall not fall, (v.3) i.e. whoever meditates in the waters of divine doctrines, produces excellent fruits. For the falling of leaves (he calls) the injuries that happen customarily. Because the Lord knows the way, i.e. (v.6) way he calls their deeds.

The 2 Psalm. Metaphorically (it refers) to the Messiah; the Jews, however, according to their insane mind refer it to Serubbabel and the house of Magog. Why do the gentiles rage, (v.1) Herod and Pilate and also the soldiers that mocked our Lord. They rage: the tumult and the clamor that came from the great mob. And the nations plot, (v.1) i.e. the priests and scribes. Vanity (v.1) he calls their vain plotting against the Messiah. They imagined that, when he was dead, he would not rise again. The kings arose, (v.2) i.e. when the sun was obscured at the time of the crucifixion, the kings of the earth arose from their thrones, seeking the reason that the heavenly lights grew dark, because from the twenty-seventh to the thirtieth of the month an eclipse, i.e. a darkening of the sun, was to take place, and especially on the twenty-eighth; this moreover, of the Lord was in the full moon; when the moon is distant from the sun, then full
is the surface of the globe. And (its) rulers, (v.2) i.e. he calls the scribes and the Pharisees because they plotted to kill him. This of the kings of each individually is cried out. Let us throw from us their yoke, (v.2) i.e. they planned to rebel and to extricate their shoulders from the yoke of the Father and the Son. The literal and spiritual interpretation of this psalm in the second column we have enlarged and made more extensive. Here then, O brother, in brevity we have treated it because of the request of those that love brevity.

The 3 Psalm. It was spoken by him when distress arose against him from Absalom. Lord, how have my oppressors increased, (v.1) i.e. oppressors he calls the band that was with Absalom. I laid down, (v.5) i.e. although I laid down for a time in distress, O Lord, yet I was awakened and delivered from them because the Lord sustained me (v.5). Upon their cheekbones, (v.7) i.e. as he that is wounded with a hard blow upon his cheeks, has his teeth shattered, thus thou wilt weaken the power of my enemies that are with Absalom. Thy blessings forever, (v.8) i.e. blessings he calls the peace which, after he had slain Absalom, (came) to the people when they returned to David.

The 4 Psalm. He admonishes those that say that the world runs by chance and that it has no one who governs it providentially. When I called upon thee, thou answeedst me, (v.1) i.e. if the world had no one who governed it, to whom have I cried and was answered? O, sons of men, how long.......,? (v.2) i.e. will you continue in this frame of mind, that is to say, that not by God I have found it, but by chance. Know that the Lord separated for himself......, (v.3) i.e. while I was still a youth and knew no one. Be angry and sin not, (v.4) i.e. although you are angry
and ponder something which is not proper against those things that are not done excellently in this world, yet you shall not abide in that thought and deprive the world of the guidance of God. Say in your hearts, (v.4) i.e. although you are justified and murmur, yet at the time of your lying down, give yourself to the meditation of beautiful things when you are by yourself. Who will show us, (v.6) i.e. where is the providence of God. ...........light......., (v.6) i.e. of his providence. Thou hast given the joy into my heart, (v.7) i.e. of his providence. Thou hast given thy joy into my heart, (v.7) i.e. not like them am I downcast, but in thee I am rejoicing and thou hast increased for me the abundance of wine and grain.

The 5 Psalm. Concerning the people in Babylon he prophesied and those that ask of God a return. Consider my sighing, (v.1) i.e. sighing he calls the severity of his pain. Give ear, O Lord, (v.1) to my eloquency, for I am praying, goaded by my pains. Lord, in the dawn......, (v.3) i.e. dawn is taken in three ways: concerning the speed and the splendor and concerning the dawn; here he speaks of the speed: with alacrity I present the prayer before thee; thou, now, with the speed of the dawn cause the light of thy salvation to shine upon me. Because thou art a God who does not take pleasure........, (v.4) i.e. therefore thou hast enabled us to go straight because we were full of crime and wickedness, and since thou dost not take pleasure in such as these, therefore thou also hatest the Babylonian(s), who are
workers of deceit, (v.5). A man that sheds blood, (v.6) i.e. Nebuchadnezzar. Their tongues are perverted, (v.9) i.e. they are deceitful to us and with lying tongues they speak with us. May they fall by......, (v.10) i.e. may they be deprived of their honor. Thou wilt bless the righteous, (v.12) i.e. the people he calls the righteous by comparison with the Babylonians.

The 7 Psalm. He spoke this psalm praising God when he heard that Ahithopel had strangled himself. From all my pursuers....., (v.1) i.e. from the evil plans of Ahithopel. May he trample down my life in the earth, (v.5) i.e. the seed of my words which he calls life so that a memory among men may not survive for me. And for its sake (return) on high, (v.7) i.e. for the sake of this that thou art doing, thou wilt be justly elevated and praised. Because he travailed with iniquity, (v.14) i.e. the evil plans. And hast brought forth wickedness, (v.14) i.e. oppression. He made a cistern and dug it, (v.15) i.e. by means of the deep intrigue that he devised. And he fell into the pit that he made, (v.15) i.e. because of this that the counsels that he counseled because for him the cause of his downfall. Upon his pate, (v.16) i.e. upon his skull. His iniquity will fall upon his head so that the roots of his hair may be continually plucked out.

The 8 Psalm. It is spoken by him concerning the incarnation of the son. Lord, our Lord, how is (thy name) glorious,
(v.1) i.e. how shalt thou come to be glorified and worshipped by the nations because thy gospel is scattered abroad in the world. Thou hast given thy glory, (v.1) i.e. may it grow and reach heaven because men will acknowledge thee that thou art the creator of heaven and earth. Because (the enemy) is put to nought, (v.2) i.e. the enemy is the Jew who sought to have vengeance, which (we read): thou art an adversary of God. Because they see thy heavens, (v.3) because the Jews did not believe thy miracles, the gentile nations acknowledge thee that thou art the creator of the heavens and the earth and the stars. What is man that thou shouldest remember him, (v.3) and the rest, i.e. the Jews interpret these (words as being) concerning Adam, we, however, concerning the Messiah.

The 9 Psalm. The praise by the people because of the victory that he gave them over the nations that surrounded them in the time of David. Thou sattest upon the throne, (v.4) like the kings that sit upon a throne and judge, so also in righteous judgment thou hast destroyed our enemy nations. A refuge for the needy....., (v.9) i.e. for the Jews because they were needy and weak in comparison with the nations. Who dwells in Zion, (v.11) i.e. it appeared that he was God by his hovering upon Zion. His schemes......, (v.11) i.e. the crafty artifices with which he tricked our enemies. To avenge their blood, (v.12) i.e. the blood of his people on them as he had promised in former times. Let the nations be judged before thee, (v.19) i.e. let them be condemned by the manifestation of
thyself against them. Raise up for them a law-giver (that they know) that they are men, (v.20) i.e. because they thought that it was impossible that he should bring them to justice. Bring upon them the punishment of thy judgment justly and lawfully that hereby they may know themselves that they are created (beings) and subjected to thy rule.

The 10 Psalm. Is spoken against the rich of the nation that oppress the needy. Why standest thou afar off, O Lord, (v.1) i.e. by this he indicates the long-suffering of God. Afar off i.e. he alludes by this to the help and not to the nature, namely: how art thou far removed from the help of the needy. The needy is incensed, (v.2) i.e. he is offended and incensed in his thought, when he sees the wicked prosper. Again, the needy is incensed seeing the arrogance of the wealthy over against him and his poverty. The wicked glories, (v.3) i.e. because he does not receive rebuke, the needy is incensed. Let them be taken in the device, (v.2) i.e. the wicked is to be called to account according to that which he has devised against the needy. The wicked is blessed, (v.3) i.e. he grows rich committing wickedness day by day. And the Lord is provoked, (v.3) i.e. do not be afraid, O needy, if the rich prosper, because the Lord is provoked at them. He lies in wait, (v.9) i.e. at all occasions the rich multiplies snares and extended nets that he may gather from the needy the possession of violence and villany. Call to account (the sin) of the evil, (v.15) i.e. his sin is
his destruction, and thou wilt not be judged because of his sin, and when he will be called to account, there will not be found an answer for him. Again when the wicked is called to account by God because of his sin, he perishes and is not found. The hope of the needy, (v.17) i.e. that prayer which for deliverance they bring to him. The preparation of their heart, (v.17) i.e. whatever they prepare to ask, thy ear will hear. To judge, (v.18) i.e. to judge and to condemn those who acted wickedly against them that not again a wicked man may destroy men from the earth.

The 11 Psalm. There was said to him when he was persecuted by Saul: flee and dwell upon the mountains, (v.1) i.e. from fear; and dwell upon....., that is, when I trust in God why do you advise that like a bird that flees from a hawk, I should depart from mountain to mountain and hide myself. For behold sinners......, (v.2) i.e. of the house of Saul. To shoot in darkness, (v.2) i.e. as in darkness without being seen they shoot their arrows at us who are orthodox. A smiting spirit, (v.6) i.e. he calls the demon, that is, by a demon spirit Saul was punished. Of their cup, (v.6) i.e. such a cup as this in the lot with the wicked was coming upon Saul: an evil demon that will torment him.

The 12 Psalm. An exhortation, and he rebuked those that deceive their friends. Because the good has come to an end, (v.1) i.e. all of those have come to an end that possess true
love. The Hebrew instead of good says pious. All of those have come to an end that are accustomed to arise manfully for truth. And faithfulness has perished, (v.1) i.e. from the inhabitants of the earth truth has departed. With a heart and a heart, (v.2) i.e. two of them deceive each other, and while they appear to agree with their mouth, they are divided in their hearts one against the other. Our tongue shall boast, (v.4) i.e. it shall speak without end. The sentence of the Lord, (v.6) i.e. the sentence of God upon the deceitful and the wicked is pure and upright and freed from deceit, like silver that is tried by the craftsmen seven times, so his judgments upon the wicked are pure. Thou wilt preserve them, (v.7) i.e. guileless. Like the licentious summit, (v.8) i.e. there is a summit in the land of the Edomites, and when they observe a festival for the idols, the men and women go out naked to the hill according to the law of heathenism, and after marching around seven times, they come upon one another as by chance and commit fornication in filth. With the licentiousness of these the prophet compares the iniquity of the sons of his generation, because there was not a ray of goodness among them, as there was also not a trace of chastity among them.

The 13 Psalm. It was spoken confessing the sin of Bathsheba. How long wilt thou forget me? (v.1) i.e. I am not saying: do not forget me, or why hast thou forgotten me, but I pray not to be forgotten forever and to be forgiven before the torments. Sorrow and misery (v.2) he calls the reflections concerning his sin which trouble and sadden him. Let (not) my enemy exalt
himself, (v.2) i.e. Absalom, and I be humbled. Enlighten my eyes, (v.3) i.e. the light of the eyes he calls the deliverance from torments. That I may not sleep, (v.4) i.e. that I may not die of torment.

The 14 Psalm. It was spoken by him in prophecy concerning Rabshaka whenSennacherib sent him to revile Hezekiah. The wicked said in his heart: there is no God, (v.1) i.e. the wicked he calls the Assyrian because of his wickedness and presumption against God because he has blotted out the knowledge of God from his heart; therefore he presumes to blaspheme. There is none that doeth good, (v.1) i.e. in his camp. They do not know, (v.4) i.e. the workers of evil who were with the Assyrian. Because God is in the generation....., (v.5) i.e. with those of the house of Hezekiah he is. There......, (v.5) i.e. round about Jerusalem. They were in fear where......, (v.5) i.e. thus the appearance of the angel terrified them where they did not expect to be harmed by anything. Who will give from Zion ...., (v.7) i.e. who else gives from the temple of Zion salvation such as this to Israel but the Lord, who turns back the captivity in the end from Babylon.

The 15 Psalm. It is like the foregoing one, for it is spoken concerning the people and concerning Hezekiah when they escaped from the Assyrians, and that they should not become proud over the victory that has come to them. Lord, why will dwell, (v.1) i.e. whom wilt thou make worthy for a dwelling and a sojourning that we also may serve and dwell with thee? and as if
God were answering. He that walketh blamelessly, (v.2) i.e. like Hezekiah. And worketh righteousness, (v.2) i.e. like him and that keeps away from evil and does the beautiful things, etc.

The 16 Psalm. A prayer of the people that it might be saved from the nations round about them. My goods are not from thee, (v.1) i.e. Hebrew: my goods are not upon thee, i.e. thou art not in need of mine, while you are gracious to me at all time. Also to the saints on earth, (v.3) i.e. scripture does not call the virtuous saints, but also those who are separated and higher than the rest in riches and rank; saints they are designated in two ways; here he calls the nations that surround them saints. And the illustrious, (v.3) i.e. those that are illustrious in wealth and power. All my desire, (v.3) i.e. I do upon them; I destroy them with my hands. There shall be increased......, (v.4) i.e. if you desire to harm me, there will be added to you other sorrows in addition to the former through the punishment and the chastisement from God. Hebrew: their idols increase, i.e. to them and to their idols I put an end that they may not further hasten to worship them. The lines are fallen......., (v.6) i.e. the good lot which came to me; it was very acceptable to me that thou hast with cords measured and divided it through Joshua Barnun. I will bless the Lord who has given us counsel, (v.7) i.e. in regard to these things, because with the giving of the land he also counseled me what I shall do
in the land through the laws which he gave me. Also in the nights there instruct me......, (v.7) i.e. also by the vexations of pains which thou dost permit to come upon me from time to time, I am instructed not a little and I receive good thoughts that cleave to God. He was at my right hand, (v.8) i.e. he sustained me with his help lest I fall by my enemies. Thou hast not given thy holy one, (v.10) i.e. many times thou hast raised as from death and corruption thy people which he calls a holy one by comparison with the nations. The true fulfillment of these (things) are understood in the Messiah and we have later interpreted it thus in a second work. Thou wilt show me the way ....., (v.11) i.e. thou hast shown me the way which, if I walk upon it, I shall find life and bliss. I shall be satisfied with the joy of thy countenance, (v.11) i.e. with thy appearance full of all blessings. And with pleasure of holiness at thy right hand, (v.11) i.e. which thy right hand has given to me.

The 17 Psalm. It was spoken concerning himself when he prayed at the time of his persecution by Saul. Thou hast proved my heart, (v.3) i.e. he shows that it is meet that his petition be heard. The great number of adversities by which he was tried he calls night, or he says this that day and night are alike to God for proving of the action. Thou hast tried me, (v.3) i.e. in the time of oppression I have been tried, but I have not turned aside from thy fear, for I have not imitated the deeds of Saul, but neither have I repeated with my mouth those things which he did to me, but in silence I have endured them. Thou hast done a miracle for thy holy ones, (v.7) i.e.
do in my salvation a miracle so that everybody will be astonished as to how I escaped from Saul. A deliverer, (v.7) i.e. make me the head and the deliverer for all those that trust in thee. I have chosen thee on my part. And from those who arise, (v.7) i.e. they, (namely) they of the house of Saul, who cast aside thy help lest it may be accomplished in me. Keep me as the apple......, (v.8) i.e. because of its weakness and its great usefulness more natural protection is provided for it than (for) all the members among the bones and the sinews and the eye-lashes and eye-lids; they guard it that they may drive away from the outside of it. In the shadow of thy wings hide me (from) those who despoil me, (v.9) the house of his father was plundered by Saul when he fled, and even his wife was given to others. The enemies of my soul who oppose me, (v.9) i.e. those who have as their characteristic sign that they will not desist from their anger unless they kill me. They praised me, (v.11) i.e. when I killed Goliath and slew the Philistine. And now they surround me, (v.11) i.e. in order to take me. And from mortals that die, (v.14) that descend to the pit and are buried like all dead and who according to thy command are covered in the earth; i.e. from such as these deliver me lest I die with them. Their belly is filled with thy treasures, (v.14) i.e. they are the decree of judgment which as in a treasure are hid for thee and laid aside and in the time when it is necessary thou wilt release them; even now reveal punishment with the sword which kills them. I, in righteousness, (v.15) i.e. I will arrive at thy help. I shall be satisfied when......, (v.15) i.e. with joy and praise. When thy faithfulness is quickened, (v.15) i.e.
when thy promises to me are confirmed by manifestly going into effect, at the time when I shall reign over all Israel.

The 18 Psalm. The praise of David for all the blessings that God did on his part all of his days. I will love thee, (v.1) i.e. as thou hast loved me and hast been to me a strength and a trust. My helper, (v.2) i.e. thou hast been to me a helper and thou hast raised up my horn against those who hate me. The pains of sheol, (v.5) i.e. many times adversities have surrounded me that bring near to death like the pains of a woman in travail. Fierce onsets of the enemies have surrounded me like the full sweep of violent torrents in April. After these things he speaks of the help of God to him and the punishment of his enemies and he composes words in a physical figure of speech. The earth was moved and trembled, (v.7) i.e. when God heard my prayer and everything at the coming was shaken by a quake and a trembling ensued; the earth and the foundations of the mountains, he calls the place in which the enemies encamped. There went up smoke in his wrath, (v.8) i.e. for when he appeared unto them, they caught fire and were burned by his revelation, i.e., smoke is the indicator of fire. And coals, (v.8) i.e. he says that after fire had overcome them, they burned and remained like coals when pieces of wood are burned. He bowed down the heaven..... and a dark cloud, (v.9) i.e. it is customary that a dark cloud gathers from the dust of warring troops; and as peace comes, whenever God appears in a light cloud, so in a dark cloud he is accustomed to be revealed to the enemies in order to throw fear into them. He made darkness...... (v.11) i.e. the devil making that darkness, whither they were cast out, (that darkness) which is by death, (that darkness) of the dark cloud under his feet, his hiding-place, (v.11) i.e. between him and them, in order that they might not see him and devise, as it
were, to flee from before him and to it. Around him is his tabernacle, (v.11) i.e. the light of his praise because it is impossible for darkness to approach him. Darkness of the water, (v.11) i.e. to that darkness which he makes his hiding-place adjoins this (darkness) and the darkness with which he conceals them is like the darkness that is seen in the clouds when they carry much rain. At the brightness, (v.12) i.e. from the beams of light, that go out from him clouds of hail and burning coals of fire, are sent forth against the enemies. And he thundered in heaven, (v.13) i.e. he ascribes the sound of thunder to God because by his command the air is shaken in these tempests. With the holy one, (v.25) i.e. not that God is like them, but he says that this is thy custom that thou rewardest the holy one according to his holiness and the upright one according to his uprightness. He will enlighten my darkness, (v.28) i.e. when I am about to become gloomy from the adversities that surround me, thou enlightenest my eyes for me. Thou hast given to me the shield, (v.35) i.e. the help of God he calls a shield which in the likeness of a shield preserves him from the arrows of the enemies. They will petition the Lord, (v.41) i.e. Lord he calls here one of the idols of the heathen. Thou wilt deliver me from the judgments of the people, (v.43) i.e. from their tumults. Thou wilt make me the head, (v.43) i.e. king over the nations. Strange sons shall disappear, (v.45) i.e. in this that they were subdued and became members of the household of God, they disappeared also from the strange paths upon which they had been running, being lame and in doubt, they were bound by the law. Lameness he calls the lack of unity of mind, like one who is lame on one foot; for by compulsion these heathen worship the God of David and not of their own free will.
God will be exalted, (v.46) i.e. he will appear lofty and glorious through the deliverance that he gave.

The 19 Psalm. Relates concerning the creations of God and his providence and foresight toward men, and he refutes those who say that the world is self-existent and that it runs fortuitously. The heavens declare, (v.1) i.e. through their height and extent they preach by silence, as if with the voice, the power of their maker. He said his praise and not his power; in as much as it is known that he is the creator, it pertains to him that he be praised. The firmament showeth, (v.1) i.e. through its height and its expanse of fluid waters. Day unto day, (v.2) i.e. even the succession of day time and night time utters every day a discourse of knowledge of their co-ordinator, that, being over against each other, they do not encroach on each other or leave their course. There is no speech nor, (v.3) i.e. he says there is no speech nor words or a word that is difficult to hear and foreign in its meaning and devoid of their teaching because they are not words that are composed of sounds, but it is knowledge which is preached silently. There is gone out their tidings, (v.4) i.e. tidings and words (spoken) with the voice he calls that knowledge of God which is shown by the creations which proclaims and teaches us eloquently by means of their construction. Upon the sun he has pitched (his tabernacle), (v.4) i.e. in the heavens, for there he has pitched a tabernacle for the sun and erected for him a house in which he might make his circuit and warm the earth below. And like a bridegroom he, (v.5) i.e. he speaks of his rise because he is of good appearance to us after darkness. To run, (v.5) i.e. unhindered he completes his course without growing weak. From
his warmth, (v.6) i.e. nothing is deprived of his heat, for behold, even the blind which are deprived of his light, bask in his warmth. The law of the Lord, (v.7) i.e. he does not refer to the law of Moses but to the knowledge that is proclaimed by the creations in as much as it is no less in value than the written law; it also educates and teaches everyone concerning God. Blameless, (v.7) i.e. faultless. Converting the soul, (v.7) i.e. of those who have erred from the true God. The testimony of the Lord, (v.7) i.e. to this very knowledge. The commandment of the Lord is choice, (v.8) i.e. tried and exalted and it enlightens the eyes (v.8) of those that are dark in their mind, hence that knowledge which (comes) from the creations he calls commandment and judgments. Just and true is this knowledge because it teaches that which proclaims concerning God. And after he spoke concerning the knowledge from creation, then he spoke of ethics. Errors, who can understand (them),? (v.12) i.e. that it is difficult for a nature, prone to evil, that anyone should escape from sin. From secret (sins), (v.12) i.e. for a man commits many things of which he does not think, and secret ones he calls these because they arise unintentionally in the thoughts of his soul, and after they are committed, we become aware that they are of the adversary, such as envy and anger and pride, and he asks God to be delivered of them because of their subtlety.

The 20 Psalm. The prayer of the people for Hezekiah that he be delivered from the Assyrians. In the day of affliction, (v.1) i.e. that of the Assyrians. And may he help thee,
(v.1) i.e. because thou hast trusted in him. God has delivered his anointed, (v.6) i.e. the greatness of the event shows that Hezekiah is his anointed and a man of God, thereby that he has been delivered of Sennacherib. May the Lord save us, (v.9) i.e. from others as now from the Assyrians. The our king might hear us, (v.9) i.e. king he calls God, as he has answered us now, he will answer us at another time.

The 21 Psalm. This was spoken personifying Hezekiah after the deliverance from the Assyrians and his recovery from the disease. May the king rejoice in thy power, O Lord, (v.1) i.e. when he was weak according to the human nature, thou didst sustain him with the victory which thou didst give him against the Assyrians. Life he asked of thee, (v.4) i.e. not only from the Assyrians hast thou saved him, but also from the disease, and life thou didst add to him. Length of days, (v.11) i.e. although in Hezekiah it was not fulfilled, yet in the Messiah it was consummated who reigns forever with his father. Great is his praise, (v.5) i.e. the greatness of his praise was this that because of his cure he turned the sun backwards, and thereby Hezekiah was praised more than by the slaughter of the Assyrians. And his joy, (v.11) i.e. by the glorious revelation joy is made perfect. Because namely they intended (evil), (v.11) i.e. they intended evil against God when they contrived to destroy his city and to demolish his temple. Thou wilt place a scar upon them, (v.12) i.e. that punishment whose scar will be preserved on them a long time. Thy preparation,
(v.12) i.e. the versicle is inverted: thy face, namely, thou hast set against them and all their preparation and their gathering thou hast scatterd.

The 22 Psalm. My God, (v.1) i.e. the prayer of David for his sin when he was pursued by Absalom. Why hast thou forsaken me, (v.1) i.e. he did not say this as complaining, but according to the custom of the righteous. And thou hast removed my salvation from me, (v.1) i.e. my sin has removed him from me. He puts a word for the deed and says: also this is sufficient to deprive me of salvation when only in words I sin. I will call to thee in the day, (v.2) i.e. I am asking for release from my distresses and it did not come to pass. They shoot out (their) lips, (v.7) i.e. they loosen their lip. From the breasts of my mother, (v.9) i.e. after the nourishment of milk and the stature of infancy; and he says that from the time of the discretion of rational speech, upon thee is my trust. The oxen and the bulls that surround him, he calls the forces that were with Absalom who were powerful and also fierce; the bulls are smaller than oxen. Dogs, again, he calls them because of their boldness. And the gathering (of the wicked), (v.16) i.e. who gathered themselves in the wickedness of their desire to destroy me when they had not been injured by me. They pierce my hands and my feet, (v.16) hereby he alludes to the severity of his sufferings and that they were prepared to do this to him if he fell into their hands. And upon my clothing, (v.18) i.e. when Absalom entered Jerusalem and committed adultery with the wives of David, he took also his garments and divided them among those who were with him. He that fear the Lord, (v.23) i.e. he is inciting others to praise: praise him, namely ye that have been chosen by him of the remnant of the nations. Esteem him highly and honor him as
he has honored you. And (your heart) shall live, (v.26) i.e. life and heart he calls the final liberation from distresses. And the seed, (v.30) i.e. not I alone will serve thee, but also the seed that shall arise after me. I exhort him that he serve him and teach the generation after him to trust in the Lord. They will come and show, (v.32) i.e. they also (will admonish) the nation that will be born of them. What the Lord does fitting to his righteousness we will speak, showing and teaching my people and the people of this people from the beginning the righteousness which the Lord has done.

The 23 Psalm. The Lord will shepherd me and (I shall not want) anything, (v.1) i.e. it is prophesied concerning the delight which came to them by the people when they returned from Babel. And upon meadows, (v.2) i.e. as he shepherded and fed me in the desert, so also now he leads me to waters in pastures of strength. Shepherds are accustomed to lead and pasture their flocks in meadows and to water. The meadows are thick grass. Thou settest before me (a table), (v.5) i.e. when they returned, Cyrus commanded that they be fed by the nations through which they passed and that with their cattle they should go to Jerusalem. Thy goodness and thy mercy, which (followed me) from Egypt, follow me from Babel, that I may return and dwell in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem forever.
